foodDescription: Cheddar, pickle, bread, butter and often ham on a board, with no cooking involved at any point. It sounds medieval and was invented in the 1950s to sell more cheese in pubs. Still the right thing to order beside a pint.

Blood sausage of pig’s blood, oats and fat, sliced and fried until the edges crisp. The town of Bury built a reputation on it and sells it hot from a market stall with mustard. Earthier and far less sweet than it sounds.

Meat cooked hard and fast in a steel wok with tomato, ginger and green chili, arriving at the table still spitting. Rusholme’s mile of Pakistani and Kashmiri restaurants has fed the city since the 1970s. Order bread, not rice.

Raw herring cured lightly in salt, served with chopped onion and pickle and eaten by holding it up by the tail. The new season’s fish arrives in June and is fattest then. Not fishy at all — sweet, soft and clean.

Fisherman’s soup, blazing red with hot paprika, made from river carp and cooked down until it stains the spoon. A Christmas Eve dish in most homes and a riverside one the rest of the year. Sweat through it with white bread.

Chicken stewed in onion and sweet paprika, finished with enough sour cream to turn the sauce orange and silky. Served with nokedli, small torn egg dumplings that exist to mop it up. Hungary’s gentlest paprika dish and its most homely.

Filled chocolates — ganache, praliné, caramel — invented in Brussels in 1912 when a pharmacist’s son put filling inside a chocolate shell. Bought by weight in a numbered box, and best eaten within days.

Flat bread slashed into a leaf shape so there is as much crust as possible, baked with olives, anchovy or bacon worked into the dough. Torn apart rather than sliced. Provence’s focaccia, drier and crustier.

Salted anchovies mashed with garlic and olive oil into a strong warm dip for raw vegetables and bread. Fishermen’s food, unapologetically salty. Served at the start of a meal with something cold to drink.

Onions cooked down for an hour until dark and sweet, in beef broth under a raft of bread and melted gruyère. Market workers ate it at dawn at the old central market. Winter only, if you want it to make sense.

Roasted eggplant and peppers cooked down with onion and tomato into a dark spread, made in huge autumn batches and jarred for the year. Eaten cold on bread. Every family’s is different and every one is defended.

The same minced meat as ćevapi pressed into one enormous flat patty, grilled hard and served in bread with onion, kajmak and ajvar. Bigger than the plate it comes on. Serbia’s answer to a burger, and older than one.

Sliced spit-roasted lamb laid over cubes of bread, drenched in tomato sauce and browned butter poured at the table, with yogurt on the side. Invented in Bursa in the 1860s and still made under that family’s name.

Macaroni, potato, cream, onion and melted cheese baked together and served with applesauce alongside, which sounds wrong and is essential. Herders’ food from the Alps, built from whatever kept well at altitude.

A pale veal sausage grilled over wood and eaten with a crusty roll and mustard, standing at a street stall. Asking for ketchup is a minor scandal, and one politician’s career only just survived doing it.

Veal sliced thin and cooked fast in a cream and white wine sauce with mushrooms, served with rösti. The city’s one signature dish, on every menu, and the standard by which local kitchens are quietly measured.

Smoked sheep’s cheese from the mountains south of the city, pressed in carved wooden molds into spindle shapes, then grilled and served with cranberry jam. Salty and firm, and it squeaks. Protected by law and seasonal.

Sauerkraut and fresh cabbage stewed for days with several meats, prunes and mushrooms, reheated over and over until it darkens. The reheating is the recipe. Hunters’ stew by name, and better every day it survives.

Slow-roasted pork neck with caraway and marjoram, sliced into a soft roll and drenched in its own cooking juices — the name comes from the word for dipping. Kraków’s own sandwich, sold from carts since the 1800s.

A honey cake of many thin layers with sour cream frosting between them, left to soften for a day before it is cut. Dense, spiced and not too sweet. Sold everywhere, and the best ones are made in somebody’s kitchen.

Hard-boiled eggs halved into a thick mustard cream sauce with potatoes. Cheap, sour and filling — a dish from the ration years that stayed on menus because people kept ordering it. Rarely found outside Germany’s east.

Beef, pork and lamb in chunks with onion, carrot and allspice, cooked in a low oven for hours with nothing but water. No browning, no thickening, no wine. Finland’s plainest stew and quietly its best-loved.

A hot dog wrapped in lompe, a soft potato flatbread, instead of a bun, with mustard, ketchup, crisp onions and sometimes shrimp salad. Sold from kiosks everywhere. Norway’s most-eaten food and the cheapest thing in the country.

Grated potato bound in a thin batter and fried into a crisp pancake, served with fried salt pork and lingonberry. Sweden’s cheapest possible hot lunch. Best where the potato is grated that morning and the edges go lacy.

Boiled pig’s trotters, sometimes crumbed and fried, eaten with your hands beside a pint. Pub food from when nothing was thrown out. Mostly gone now, kept alive by a few places doing it deliberately. Sticky, salty, mostly gelatin.

Potatoes stewed slowly with onion, dripping and yesterday’s roast meat until it all collapses together. Made from leftovers, so no two are the same. Served with oatcakes, and at funerals and weddings in vast quantities.

Sheep’s heart, liver and lungs minced with oats, onion and a lot of pepper, cooked in a casing and served with mashed turnip and potato. Peppery and warm, and far less alarming than the description. Whisky sauce is a modern touch.

A flat orange-scented sponge under heavy powdered sugar, stenciled with the city’s lily crest and cut into squares. Made for Carnival in February and gone by Lent. Some bakeries fill it with cream, which is an improvement.

Flatbread dimpled with fingertips, drenched in olive oil and coarse salt and baked until the base crisps while the top stays soft. Sold by weight in bakeries and split for sandwiches. The name means squashed.

The cow’s fourth stomach, simmered with tomato and herbs, chopped into a bun whose top is dipped in the cooking broth, with green sauce and chili. Sold from carts since the 1400s. Florence’s real street food, and still cheap.

A double-crusted tart of sheep’s-milk ricotta and sour cherries from the bakeries of the Jewish quarter. The pastry lid hides the filling, said to have begun as a way around a rule against selling dairy sweets.

Lacy fritters of chickpea flour and tiny whole shrimp, fried so thin the edges shatter. The shrimp go in raw, shells and all, hundreds to a fritter. From the salt marshes near Cádiz, perfected in Seville’s bars.

Oxtail stewed with red wine, carrots and cloves until the meat slides off the bone into the sauce. It came from the bullring, where the animal was eaten after the fight. Rich enough that it should end the day’s eating.

Small fish — anchovy, red mullet, cuttlefish — floured and dropped into hot olive oil for barely a minute, so the coating stays pale and the fish steams inside. Served in a paper cone with lemon. Andalusia’s best trick.

Bread soaked in milk and sweet wine, dipped in egg, fried, and dusted with cinnamon sugar. Spain’s Easter answer to French toast, in every bakery through Lent and gone by May. Denser and boozier than it looks.

Pig’s ear boiled, sliced and seared hard on a flat grill with garlic and paprika, crisp at the edges and gelatinous in the middle. A texture more than a flavor. Order it with a beer and stop thinking about it.

Tripe stewed for hours with chorizo, blood sausage and paprika until the sauce goes sticky and the tripe turns tender. Organ meat, unapologetically. Madrid’s oldest restaurant dish and still the test of a serious tavern.

Fresh unsalted curd cheese under a pour of honey, sometimes with walnuts. Three ingredients, no technique, and Catalonia’s oldest dessert — older than sugar reaching Europe. The cheese should taste of milk and nothing else.

A fat pork sausage grilled over coals with white beans fried in the same pan so they take on the fat. Catalonia’s plainest and most-eaten plate. No sauce, no garnish — a good sausage does not need either.

Vienna’s answer to Hungarian goulash, and a different dish entirely: no vegetables, no soup, just beef and its own weight in onions cooked down to a thick paprika gravy. The Fiaker version arrives with a fried egg and a sausage on top.

Dense savory rings made with lard, black pepper and whole almonds — nothing like the sweet kind. Bought by the bag along the seafront and eaten with cold beer while looking at the bay. The pepper heat builds slowly.

Lamb on the bone simmered with potato, carrot, rutabaga and herbs into a clear, plain, restorative soup. Iceland’s answer to its weather. Nothing about it is fancy, and everyone has a grandmother whose version was better.

Boiled white fish and potato mashed together with butter, milk and onion into something between a stew and a mash. Nursery food, invented to use up yesterday’s catch and still cooked weekly at home. Eat it on dark rye with butter.

Clear caraway schnapps, unsweetened and blunt, nicknamed “black death” for the old black label. Drunk cold in a shot beside fermented shark, on the theory that each makes the other survivable. Iceland’s only real spirit tradition.

Small anise doughnuts sold for the city’s patron saint in mid-May, in four versions: plain, sugar-glazed, meringue-topped, and the ones called “French”. The plain ones are the good ones. Two weeks a year, then nothing.

White beans stewed with tomato, garlic and sage — cooked, the saying goes, the way you would cook small birds. Tuscans eat so many beans that other Italians call them “bean-eaters”. Ordered as a side and eaten as a meal.

A sour wheat beer, low in alcohol and tart enough to make you blink, traditionally cut with raspberry or woodruff syrup and served in a wide bowl of a glass. Napoleon’s troops called it “the Champagne of the north”.

Veal rolled around kajmak, breaded and fried, then served with tartar sauce — a 1950s invention nicknamed “the maiden’s dream”, for reasons that become obvious. Enormous, molten inside, and entirely unserious.

The real thing is a soup, not a stew: beef, onion, potato and a great deal of paprika, thin enough to drink, traditionally cooked outdoors in a kettle over fire. What English calls “goulash” is closer to Hungary’s pörkölt. Order it as a first course.

Haddock, not cod, in batter with chips, wrapped and eaten hot. In Glasgow a “supper” means it comes with chips; a “single fish” means without. Many city chip shops were opened by Italian immigrant families, and some still are. Salt and vinegar on top.

A spiced fruit pudding of flour, suet, dried fruit and treacle, wrapped in a cloth — a “cloot” — and boiled for hours until it forms a dark, shiny skin. Sliced and eaten with custard, or fried for breakfast next morning. Made at Christmas and birthdays.

Grilled marinated chicken in a spiced tomato and cream sauce, invented in Britain rather than India, most likely by a Bangladeshi cook adapting to local taste. A foreign secretary once called it “a true British national dish”.

A whole meat and potato pie put inside a buttered bread roll — carbohydrate wrapped in carbohydrate, known locally as a “Wigan kebab”. Sold in bakeries at breakfast. There is no defense of it, and none is required.

A thin cut of beef seared rare under a pat of herb butter, with a mound of thin fries and no vegetable in sight. Order it “saignant” and expect it rarer than you meant. The fries are usually refilled without asking.

Split pea soup cooked with pork until a spoon will stand up in it, with smoked sausage sliced through. Also called “snert”. Traditionally eaten after skating on frozen canals, and only correct when genuinely thick.

Juniper spirit aged in oak, the ancestor of gin, poured brimming into a tulip glass that you bend down to sip without lifting. Ordered beside a beer, a pairing called a “headbutt”. Ask for oude, the maltier kind.

Half anchovy and half cheese on a thin base from a wood oven, sold from vans since Italian families arrived a century ago. Ask for “half and half” and you will be understood. Emmental rather than mozzarella, which is the local way.

Czech lager poured slowly under a thick wet head that is part of the drink rather than a mistake — ask for a “hladinka” and you get the standard pour. Czechs drink more beer per person than anyone, and it costs less than water.

A round doughnut with no hole, filled with jam and dusted in sugar. In Berlin it is a “Pfannkuchen”; everywhere else it is a “Berliner”, and locals will correct you. Eaten at New Year, sometimes filled with mustard as a prank.

Flat pork and beef patties with soaked bread, onion and marjoram, fried and eaten cold with mustard as often as hot. The Berlin word for what the rest of Germany calls a “Frikadelle”. Sold at bakeries and old corner pubs.

What the rest of the world calls “Danish pastry”: laminated dough with butter folded in dozens of times, filled with custard or jam. Danes named it for Vienna, where the technique came from. Buy it before ten in the morning.

Smoked haddock, potato, onion and milk cooked into a thick soup. “Skink” is an old word for broth, and Cullen is the fishing village it comes from. Smoky, plain and entirely warming, with bread and butter alongside.

Sweet red vermouth poured from a tap over ice, with an olive and a twist of orange. Sunday before lunch is the appointed hour, and “going for a vermut” means the whole ritual rather than the drink. Most bars blend their own.

A shell of paper-thin pastry layers, ridged like a fan, filled with ricotta, semolina and candied citrus. “Riccia” is the crisp version, “frolla” the soft one. Buy it hot in the morning, while the shell still shatters when you bite.

Langoustines, called “lobster” here although they are neither — smaller and sweeter, usually split and grilled in garlic butter or turned into a thick bisque. The best come from the southeast coast. Expensive, and worth it once.

Dense, dark, faintly sweet rye baked slowly underground using geothermal heat, which earns it the nickname “thunder bread”. Sliced thin and buttered heavily, usually under smoked fish. Sweeter than any rye bread you have had before.

An Icelandic hot dog, mostly lamb, snapping in a soft bun under raw and crisp fried onions, ketchup, sweet brown mustard and remoulade. Ask for “eina með öllu” — one with everything. The harbor stand has sold them since 1937.

Sour-cherry liqueur, sweet and sticky, poured at stand-up counters since 1840. Ask for it “com elas” — with them — and the boozy cherries come in the glass. A euro or so, one shot, drunk on the sidewalk. A pre-dinner ritual, not a dessert.

Pork liver marinated in wine, vinegar and garlic, then flash-fried — “with them” means the boiled potatoes alongside. Old Lisbon food from when organ meat was the cheap cut. Sour, iron-rich, strong. Order it where the tablecloths are paper.

Octopus boiled tender, then roasted until the edges crisp and drenched in olive oil — “lagar” means olive press — with smashed potatoes and whole garlic cloves. Portugal eats more octopus per person than almost anywhere. The oil is the sauce.

Tiny snails simmered with garlic, oregano and piri-piri chili, served by the bowlful with cold beer from May to August. A sign reading “Há caracóis” — we have snails — means the season is open. Pull each one out with a toothpick, then drink the broth.

Helles and clear lemon soda, half and half. Franz Xaver Kugler claimed to have invented it in 1922 for cyclists at his inn south of Munich — “Radler” means cyclist — though the word appears in print earlier. Sold by the Maß in beer gardens.

A veal chop on the bone, dipped in egg and breadcrumbs and fried in clarified butter. Milan and Vienna argue over who came first, this or the Wiener Schnitzel. The version beaten out to the size of the plate is called “orecchia d’elefant”, elephant’s ear.

Tripe cut into fine strips and simmered with white beans, carrot, celery and tomato, then finished with Parmigiano. Once the meal after midnight mass on Christmas Eve. Other Italians used to call the Milanese “busecconi”, tripe eaters, and it stuck.

Flattened meatballs of leftover boiled meat, mortadella or salami, milk-soaked bread and Parmigiano, fried in butter. The name is traced to the Spanish “albóndiga”. Thrift food turned bar food: look for them on aperitivo counters around six.

Tendons and cartilage from calves’ knees, boiled for hours, pressed, sliced thin and dressed with raw onion, oil and vinegar, sometimes with beans. Cold, chewy and translucent. A fixture of old osterie, where it is listed in dialect as “gnervitt”.

A tall domed loaf of butter, eggs, candied orange and raisins, raised over days from a natural starter. Legend credits a kitchen boy named Toni at the Sforza court: “pan de Toni”. Keep a slice for 3 February, San Biagio’s day, said to protect the throat.

Campari and red vermouth topped with sparkling wine instead of gin. The story goes that Mirko Stocchetto, owner of Bar Basso, picked up the wrong bottle in the early 1970s. The bar still serves it, in an outsized goblet. “Sbagliato” means mistaken.

Soda bread dough patted into a round, cut in four and cooked on a dry griddle rather than baked, so it comes out flat, floury and soft inside. “Farl” is from an old word for a quarter. Split it, fry it, and fill it with bacon or an egg.

Mashed potato kneaded with flour and butter, rolled thin and cut into triangles, then browned on a griddle. Also called “fadge” or “tattie bread”. Unlike boxty it uses cooked potato only. Fried in butter it goes crisp and chewy at the same time.

A pastie here is no Cornish pasty: it is a round patty of minced pork, onion and potato, battered and deep-fried. “Supper” means it comes with chips. A Belfast chip shop order that needs salt, vinegar and nothing more complicated.

Lamb or beef stewed for hours with potatoes, onions and carrots until the potatoes break down and thicken it. Named after “lobscouse”, a sailors’ stew, and the source of the city’s nickname. Eat it with pickled red cabbage or beetroot and buttered bread.

Hard butter toffee first sold in the 1700s by Molly Bushell in Everton, then a village above the docks. It gave Everton FC its nickname, “the Toffees”, and before home games a Toffee Lady still throws Everton mints, striped boiled sweets, into the crowd.

White bread, butter and strawberry jam, folded or cut in half; a “butty” is any sandwich here. Comedian Ken Dodd, from the Knotty Ash district, spent a career joking about the jam butty mines worked by his Diddy Men. Best with a mug of tea.

A Glasgow morning roll, floury and soft with a crust that shatters, split and filled with a slice of square sausage, also called “Lorne”. The local hangover breakfast. Add a fried egg or tattie scone, and choose red sauce or brown — people do care.

A bright orange fizzy drink made by AG Barr, a Glasgow firm, since 1901, now produced in Cumbernauld. Sweet, faintly of bubblegum and citrus, with a secret recipe. Scots drink it as a hangover cure. A Glaswegian may call any fizzy drink “ginger”.

A pale, crisp lager brewed at the Wellpark Brewery in the city’s East End, beside the Necropolis cemetery, where Tennent’s began making lager in 1885. The default pint in almost every Glasgow pub. Ask for a pint of Tennent’s and nobody will ask which size.

Glasgow’s word for an ice cream cone, sold from ice cream vans and from the cafés opened by Italian families who arrived from the late 1800s. Vanilla is standard. Ask for a ninety-nine and you get a chocolate flake pushed in the top.

A round shortbread biscuit topped with a dome of soft white marshmallow and coated in thin milk chocolate, in red and silver foil. Made by Tunnock’s in Uddingston, east of the city, since 1956. Giant dancing versions opened the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Minced beef stewed slowly with onion and carrot until it turns into thick gravy, served with plain boiled or mashed potatoes. The everyday Glasgow dinner for generations. Unglamorous, comforting, and still on the menu in old-fashioned cafés.

A Scotch pie of spiced mutton or beef, eaten with a cup of Bovril — a hot, salty beef-extract drink — at half time on the terraces. The standard winter ritual at Celtic Park, Ibrox and Hampden. Hold the pie upright or the grease goes everywhere.

Macaroni cheese baked inside a hot-water pastry case, sometimes browned on top under extra cheddar. Carbohydrate inside carbohydrate, sold warm in Glasgow bakeries and at football grounds. Locals eat them cold too, straight from the paper bag.

Mashed potato kneaded with flour and butter, rolled thin, cut into triangles and cooked dry on a griddle. Fried again in the pan for a Scottish breakfast, or folded into a roll with square sausage. Supermarkets sell them in packs; bakeries’ are better.

Haggis, the peppery Scottish pudding of sheep’s offal and oats, broken into pieces, dipped in spiced chickpea batter and fried. A Glasgow curry-house starter that joins the city’s two food traditions. Served with a sweet red chilli dip or mint yogurt.

A cheese and tomato pizza, usually halved, dipped in fish batter and deep-fried until the crust crackles and the cheese runs. A Glasgow chip shop staple, ordered as a supper with chips. Eat it standing up, quickly, while the batter is still crisp.

A pizza box filled with whatever the takeaway has: doner meat, chicken pakora, chips, onion rings, garlic bread, naan, salad and several sauces, all piled together. Bought late at night from Glasgow’s Indian and Pakistani takeaways, and meant for sharing.

Grilled chicken tikka in a creamy, mildly spiced tomato sauce. Glasgow’s claim: in the early 1970s Ali Ahmed Aslam at the Shish Mahal restaurant improvised the sauce, tomato soup included, for a diner who found his chicken dry. London disputes it.

Hard, flat ginger biscuits sold at the market in Ormskirk, a Lancashire market town just north of the city, where they have been made since the 1700s. Sold by the bag. They snap rather than bend and are best dunked in tea, the ginger arriving slowly.

Asparagus grown in the sandy coastal soil at Formby, north of Liverpool, a market-garden crop there for over a century. The season is short, roughly May and June. Eat it simply, with butter or a soft egg, and buy it from farm stands while it lasts.

Tiny brown shrimps from the sands off Southport, a seaside town north of the city, packed into pots under butter spiced with mace and nutmeg. Spread on hot toast so the butter melts. A Victorian seaside treat, still at fishmongers and on older menus.

Plain, dry, flaky crackers made by Jacob’s at its Aintree factory, north of the city, since 1914, near the racecourse where the Grand National is run. Eaten with butter and cheese. Trying to eat several without a drink is an old playground challenge.

The two old Liverpool beers. Higsons bitter was the city’s pint for generations until the brewery closed in 1990; the name has since been revived. Cains brewed at the red-brick brewery on Stanhope Street. Try one in a Victorian pub like the Philharmonic.

Minced beef, onion and potato in shortcrust, the matchday lunch around the football grounds. The best known come from Homebaked, the co-operative bakery on Oakfield Road opposite Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium. On match days they sell out before kick-off.

The Friday tea from the chip shop: fish or a pie, chips, mushy peas and, here, curry sauce or gravy over the top. Many chippies here are Chinese-run, so the curry sauce is the takeaway kind. A chip butty, chips in a buttered roll, is the cheap option.

Steamed dumplings, char siu pork buns and egg tarts in the restaurants around Nelson Street in Chinatown, under its ceremonial arch. The community dates to the 1860s, when the Blue Funnel shipping line began sailing to China. Go at weekend lunchtime.

Chips fried crisp, then tossed in a wok with salt, chilli, onion, peppers and five-spice. Liverpool’s Chinese takeaways claim them, and the city has Europe’s oldest Chinese community, so the claim holds up. Eat them fast, before the steam turns them soft.

A shortcrust tart filled with a whole lemon, peel and all, cooked down with brown sugar, butter and egg. Sharper and darker than a French lemon tart, with a faint bitterness from the rind. An old home recipe, now mostly found in cookbooks and the odd café.

A dense slab of bread pudding or leftover cake, packed with dried fruit and soaked in syrup until it sags. The name is usually traced to Lord Nelson, via a richer Nelson cake. Heavy, sticky and cheap, a bakery staple. Eat it warm, with custard if offered.

Scouse with no meat in it, made at the end of the week or the end of the money from potatoes, onions, carrots and stock. Still cooked at home and in some cafés. Thinner than the real thing and not pretending otherwise; the pickled cabbage does the work.

A dark, sticky malted loaf that has almost disappeared everywhere except Northern Ireland. Sold sliced in supermarkets, it is eaten toasted with plenty of butter and often a slice of cheese. Slightly sweet, slightly bitter, and best toasted.

Northern Ireland’s own Tayto, made since 1956 at Tandragee Castle in County Armagh and unrelated to the Tayto brand in the Republic. Cheese and onion is the flagship flavour. A crisp sandwich in buttered white bread is a respected local lunch.

Irish whiskey from the Old Bushmills Distillery on the north Antrim coast, which points to a 1608 royal licence to distil in the area. Triple-distilled and smooth. Ask for it neat or with a drop of water; Belfast bars stock several ages of it.

The first new potatoes of the year, grown in the light soil around Comber in County Down and with protected-name status since 2012. Thin-skinned and waxy, in shops from early summer. Boil them, add butter and salt, and that is the whole recipe.

Red seaweed gathered off the north Antrim coast and dried until leathery, then eaten straight from the bag as a salty snack. Traditionally paired with yellowman at the Lammas Fair. Look for it at St George’s Market. The taste is the sea, concentrated.

Hard, golden honeycomb toffee made with golden syrup and baking soda, broken off the block with a hammer. Sold most famously at the Ould Lammas Fair in Ballycastle each August. Gets into your teeth and stays there; that is part of the deal.

A domed bun between bread and sponge cake, with a crackled sugar top and sometimes a cherry or a few currants. Despite the name it has nothing to do with France. A Belfast bakery staple, cut in half and buttered by those who think it needs it.

A no-bake traybake of fifteen crushed digestive biscuits, fifteen marshmallows and fifteen glacé cherries, bound with condensed milk and rolled in coconut. Chilled and sliced. Sold in every café cabinet and nobody has ever needed a recipe card for it.

A ring doughnut, fried and rolled in sugar, under the name every Northern Irish bakery uses. Plain dough, no filling, no icing. Best still warm from the fryer, with a cup of tea, and a napkin for the sugar that will end up down your front.

A big, round, soft white roll dusted in flour, with a dark crust on top that looks close to burnt. Bakeries pile them in the window. Split one for a bacon or sausage bap, or for a pastie bap, which is exactly what it sounds like.

Mashed potato beaten with hot milk and chopped scallions, piled up with a well of butter melting in the middle. Not colcannon, which has cabbage or kale; Ulster cooks will explain the difference unasked. Served beside sausages or boiled ham.

Bacon, sausage, egg and black pudding, but what makes it Ulster is the bread: a soda farl and a slice of potato bread, both fried in the pan fat until golden. Beans are a point of dispute. Eaten late morning, followed by nothing until dinner.

Fruit simmered in water with a little sugar and served cold in a glass, often with the fruit still in it: strawberries in summer, apples and plums in autumn. The default drink with a milk-bar lunch. Home versions vary wildly in sweetness.

A pink-and-white chewy sugar sweet, made in Praga since the 19th century. Sold from stalls outside Warsaw cemeteries such as Powązki on All Saints’ Day, 1 November. It sticks to your teeth; that is the point.

Melted chocolate rather than cocoa, thick enough to stand a spoon in, served in Wedel’s chocolate lounges, the oldest on Szpitalna Street in the city centre. Order it plain or with chilli and expect to finish with a spoon. A glass of water helps.

Squares of soft vanilla mousse coated in chocolate, invented by Warsaw chocolatier Jan Wedel in 1936. The name is from the saying that a rich man has everything but bird’s milk. Sold in every corner shop; the vanilla box is the original.

Chocolate sponge soaked in punch, layered with thick whipped cream and covered in chocolate glaze. Created in Warsaw around 1950, most likely named after the W-Z route, the postwar east–west road through the rebuilt centre. Eat it with a fork, carefully.

Raw chopped beef with a raw egg yolk on top, surrounded by diced pickles, onion and pickled mushrooms that you mix in yourself. A starter in old restaurants and a vodka snack in all-night bars. The yolk may come in its half-shell so you can add it slowly.

Salted herring in oil with raw onion, or in sour cream with apple, eaten as a zakąska, a bite between shots of vodka. Warsaw’s late-night bars serve it for a few złoty a plate, the Polish currency. One shot, one bite is the rhythm.

Thin pancakes folded around sweetened curd cheese, jam or fruit, sometimes fried again in butter and topped with cream. A cheap lunch rather than a dessert in milk bars like Prasowy on Marszałkowska Street. Savoury versions come with spinach or mushrooms.

Grated potato and onion fried in thin, crisp-edged pancakes. Eaten with sour cream or sugar, or folded around goulash as placek po węgiersku, Hungarian-style. A milk-bar classic; the ones fried to order beat the ones sitting under the lamp.

A cold summer soup of young beetroot and its leaves stirred into kefir or soured milk with cucumber, radish and dill, usually topped with half a boiled egg. Shocking pink and sharp. Only on menus in hot months, so order it when you see it.

Tomato soup made on the stock left from Sunday’s chicken broth, with rice or thin noodles and a swirl of sour cream. The Monday soup of every Polish household and every milk bar. Sweeter and creamier than a Spanish or Italian version, and cheap everywhere.

Cabbage leaves wrapped around minced pork and rice, baked or simmered and served under tomato or mushroom sauce. The name means little pigeons, and nobody can say why. A milk-bar staple and a home-cooking test: the leaf should cut with a fork.

Thin beef slices rolled around pickled cucumber, bacon and onion, tied with string and braised soft in dark gravy. Served with buckwheat groats or mashed potato. Old-school Warsaw restaurants keep them on the menu. Check for the string before you bite.

Pork loin beaten thin, breaded and fried in lard until the edges curl, served with boiled potatoes and dill and a side of cabbage or cucumber salad. The Polish Sunday lunch. Milk bars do a cheap and honest one; the plate rarely leaves room for dessert.

Round dumplings of grated raw and boiled potato, often stuffed with minced meat, served under fried onion and pork crackling. A Praga dish: women once sold them hot from jars at Bazar Różyckiego, the old east-bank market. Heavy, so plan a walk after.

A half-moon of dough filled with tomato and mozzarella and fried until it puffs. Puglian by origin, made a Milanese habit by Luini, the bakery just off the Duomo square since 1949. The queue moves fast. Eat it on the pavement and mind the molten middle.

The bright red bitter that Gaspare Campari created in 1860 and his family went on to make in Milan. His son Davide opened the Camparino bar in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II arcade in 1915. Order a Campari Seltz at the counter there, standing up.

Hot chocolate and coffee whipped with milk into a froth, drunk hot in winter and cold in summer. Named after Domenico Barbaja, a Milanese café waiter who became the great opera impresario of the 1800s, running La Scala and the San Carlo in Naples.

Sweet cornmeal buns scented with dried elderflower and dusted with sugar. Made for 23 April, the feast of St George, patron of Milan’s dairymen, and once eaten dipped in fresh cream. The name means millet bread, after the flour it was first made with.

A puffed white roll stamped with a star pattern, almost entirely crust and air, descended from the Austrian Kaisersemmel brought in under Habsburg rule. Good ones are getting rarer. Split one and fill it with mortadella, or with a slab of cotoletta.

A thick soup of beans, cabbage, courgette, potato and whatever else is in season, made in Milan with rice rather than pasta and often a piece of pork rind for depth. In summer it is served at room temperature, which is how many locals prefer it.

Pork ribs, rind, trotters and small sausages stewed with Savoy cabbage, best after the first frost. A winter dish, traditionally started around 17 January, the feast of St Anthony the Abbot. Served with polenta, followed by a long walk.

A thick cross-cut of veal shank braised slowly in white wine and stock until the meat comes off the bone, topped with gremolata: chopped lemon zest, garlic and parsley. The marrow in the middle is the prize, and some places bring a small spoon for it.

Rice toasted in butter with onion and beef marrow, cooked slowly in stock and turned deep gold with saffron, then finished with butter and Parmigiano. A popular legend credits a glassworker at the Duomo in 1574. Order it with ossobuco.

A full litre in a heavy glass mug, the beer garden standard. Augustiner, Munich’s oldest brewery, is the local favorite. In the self-service area you may bring your own food, a right dating to 1812, but you buy the drinks there.

Cloudy, fizzy beer brewed with wheat, tasting of banana and clove from the yeast. Poured slowly into a tall curved glass. For centuries only Bavaria’s rulers had the right to brew it. Drunk in the morning with Weißwurst without anyone remarking on it.

Munich’s everyday beer: pale gold, soft and mildly bitter, first brewed by Spaten in 1894 to compete with Pilsner. Ask for “a Helles” in any beer garden and this is what comes. Lighter in taste than in alcohol.

Seven thin sponge layers with chocolate buttercream under a dark chocolate glaze, created in Munich for Prince Regent Luitpold, who ruled Bavaria from 1886. The seven layers are said to stand for Bavaria’s seven districts of the time.

A yeast pastry pulled by hand into a thin, see-through middle with a thick ring, then fried in lard and dusted with sugar. Traditionally stretched over the knee. The Schmalznudel café at the Viktualienmarkt market fries them from early morning.

A ball of yeast dough cooked in a covered pan with milk and butter, so it steams soft on top and caramelizes to a salty crust underneath. Served with vanilla sauce. A main course on meatless Fridays in older Bavarian households.

A large white radish cut into a spiral, salted and left until it weeps. Eaten raw and peppery alongside beer, often on a wooden board as part of a Brotzeit. Sold by the piece at beer gardens, some still cut by hand to order.

Whole mackerel or whitefish, spiced, threaded on a wooden stick and grilled slowly beside charcoal. Eaten with your hands at beer gardens and at the Oktoberfest, with a Brezn. Look for the long grill with rows of fish standing in it.

Pork shoulder roasted with its rind scored, basted with dark beer, and served in its gravy with a potato or bread dumpling and cabbage salad. The Bavarian Sunday lunch, and on nearly every Wirtshaus menu every day of the week.

A whole pork knuckle roasted slowly until the skin blisters into hard crackling and the meat falls off the bone. Served with dark beer gravy and a potato dumpling. One per person, and it is a lot. The beer halls’ signature plate.

A fine-ground loaf of pork and beef baked until the top crusts brown. Despite the name there is no liver and no cheese in the Bavarian version. Cut in thick slabs and put in a roll with mustard as a Leberkässemmel, the city’s standing-up lunch.
Ripe Camembert mashed with butter, sweet paprika, onion and caraway, sometimes with a splash of beer. A beer garden staple, spread thick on a Brezn or rye bread. The name means mashed-up in Bavarian.

Bavaria’s pretzel: a fat, soft belly and thin crisp arms, dipped in lye before baking for the dark glossy crust and scattered with coarse salt. Split and buttered it becomes a Butterbrezn. Beer gardens sell them as big as a plate.

Veal and pork sausage flavored with parsley and lemon, kept warm in water and peeled at the table. Eaten before noon with sweet mustard, a Brezn and a wheat beer — the Weißwurstfrühstück. Tradition says it should never hear the midday bells.

White peach purée topped with Prosecco, invented by Giuseppe Cipriani at Harry’s Bar near St Mark’s in 1948 and named for the painter Giovanni Bellini, for its pink colour. Harry’s Bar still serves it, at Harry’s Bar prices.

A small glass of house wine, drunk standing at the counter, often well before noon. The name means shade: wine sellers in St Mark’s Square are said to have moved their stalls with the bell tower’s shadow to keep the wine cool.

White wine, a bitter liqueur and a splash of soda over ice, with an olive or a slice of orange. The name goes back to Austrian soldiers in the 1800s who added water to local wine. Venetians often order it with Select, a bitter first made here in 1920.

Thin, dry oval biscuits named after the young sea bass they’re said to resemble. Baked twice so they would keep for months at sea. Dunked in coffee, hot chocolate or sweet wine, and still sold in tins by Venetian bakers.

Coffee-soaked sponge fingers layered with mascarpone whipped with egg and sugar, dusted with cocoa. Younger than it seems: most accounts place its invention in Treviso, 30 km north, around the 1970s, though Friuli disputes that. Venice adopted it anyway.

Fried dough balls rolled in sugar, sold in the weeks before Lent. The Venetian kind has raisins and pine nuts; others are filled with zabaglione or cream. Under the Republic, fritter-makers had their own guild.

Calf’s liver cut into thin strips and cooked fast in a pan of onions that have already been softened slowly, finished with parsley. Served with polenta. The onions are as much the point as the liver, and there are a lot of them.

Cuttlefish stewed in their own ink, usually with white wine, until the sauce is jet black. Served with soft white polenta, which is the Venetian kind. It stains your teeth for a while afterwards, and nobody minds.

Rice cooked with young spring peas and a stock made from their pods, looser than risotto and eaten with a spoon. It was served to the doge on 25 April, the feast of St Mark, when the first peas came in from the lagoon gardens.

foodEnglishName: Thick pasta with onion and anchovy
foodDescription: Thick whole-wheat strands pushed through a hand-cranked press, tossed with onions cooked down slowly with salted anchovies or sardines. No cheese. Once food for lean days, and still eaten on Christmas Eve and Good Friday.

Small lagoon crabs caught in the few days they shed their shells, in spring and again in autumn. They go live into beaten egg, which they eat, then are floured and fried whole. A shrinking number of lagoon fishermen still do the work.

Dried cod soaked for days, poached, then beaten with olive oil until pale and fluffy, spread on bread or grilled polenta. Despite the name it’s made from air-dried stockfish, a taste traced to a Venetian merchant shipwrecked in Norway in 1432.

Fried sardines layered with onions stewed soft in vinegar, plus raisins and pine nuts, then left a day or more to soak. A sailors’ way of keeping fish for a voyage. Eaten cold, and traditionally on the night of the Redentore festival in July.

Soft white crustless bread folded around fillings piled so high the middle bulges: tuna and egg, shrimp, ham and mushroom. Kept in glass cases on bar counters from morning on. The Venetian version is known for that bulge.

Small snacks lined up on the counter of a bacaro: crostini, fried meatballs, half an egg with an anchovy, salami on grilled polenta. Point at what you want, eat standing, pay by the piece. For plenty of Venetians this is dinner.

The everyday Portuguese lunch: a thin steak under a fried egg, with rice, fries and a buttery wine pan sauce. Break the yolk so it runs into the rice — that is the whole point. About €10 with a glass of wine, and the truest test of a cheap diner.

Soupy tomato, cilantro and shellfish rice, brought to the table in its pot and ladled out wet rather than fluffy. A coastal Sunday dish that became a restaurant classic. Usually serves two and takes half an hour — order it as soon as you sit down.

Green beans in a light, blistered batter — little fish of the garden — invented for days when the church banned meat. Portuguese missionaries carried the technique to Japan, where it became tempura. Eat them hot with lemon, before the batter softens.

Garlicky beef steak slapped into a bread roll, traditionally the last thing you order at a seafood meal — after the shellfish, not instead of it. In the old beer halls it arrives as dessert. Mustard and piri-piri chili sauce; never well done.

Croquettes of salt cod, potato and parsley, shaped between two spoons into a small football and fried until the ridges crisp. Cheap counter food since the 1800s, eaten warm or cold with a beer. Skip the cheese-stuffed ones sold to tourists.

Small clams steamed open in olive oil with unreasonable amounts of garlic, cilantro and lemon. Named for a 19th-century poet who loved them. The broth is the point: scoop it up with an empty shell, then mop the bowl clean with bread.

Thin pork cutlets simmered in white wine, garlic and bay leaf, stuffed into a plain bread roll that soaks up the juice. The Lisbon version is wet and pale rather than grilled. Order it with mustard and a beer, eat at the counter, take napkins.

Warm custard tart in shatter-crisp pastry, the top blistered almost black. When Portugal shut down its monasteries in 1834, the monks sold these to survive; the original bakery still guards the recipe. Eat it standing, minutes out of the oven.

Whole oily sardines charred over coals, fattest and best from June to August. During the Santo António street festivals in June, the Alfama quarter fills with grills and smoke. Eat them with your fingers off a slice of bread — then eat the bread.

Shredded salt cod tangled with matchstick fries and onion, loosely bound in barely-set egg, black olives and parsley on top. Named for the Lisbon tavern keeper who invented it. It should be creamy — if it is firm like an omelet, it sat too long.

A sugar-dusted puff-pastry pillow filled with almond and egg cream, baked at the Piriquita bakery since 1862 and worth the train ride to Sintra. Eat one hot while the line is out the door, then take home a box of queijadas, small cheese tarts.

Lamb smoked over birch and, traditionally, dried sheep dung, sliced cold onto flatkaka: a soft rye flatbread cooked dark on a griddle. Christmas food that shops sell all year. Salty, smoky, and the most Icelandic thing you can hold.

Cod or haddock hung in the sea wind until it dries into stiff, protein-dense sheets, torn into strips and eaten under a thick layer of butter. Sold in every supermarket as a snack. Smells alarming, tastes clean and faintly sweet.

Greenland shark buried, fermented and hung for months, which is what makes it edible — fresh, the meat is poisonous. Ammonia on the nose, oily on the tongue, served in cubes with a toothpick. A dare, honestly, and chased with schnapps.

A knot of cardamom-scented dough fried in fat, crisp outside and dense within. The bakery item every Icelandic household keeps in a tin, and the thing offered the moment you sit down. Not sweet enough to be a doughnut, which is the point.

Soft-serve blended with candy, cookies or fruit into a thick swirl, eaten year-round in defiance of the weather — Icelanders line up for ice cream in February. The name means trickster fox. Pick two mix-ins and regret nothing.

A paper cone of whatever the fryer has going — anchovies, squid, zucchini flowers, rice balls — handed over scalding and eaten while walking. Street food in its purest form. Salt it yourself and do not ask what everything is.

Not a meat sauce but whole cuts of beef and pork collapsed into tomato over five or six hours until the sauce goes dark and the meat falls apart. Sunday cooking. The pasta arrives first, the meat after it, as a second course.

A fistful of cooked pasta bound with béchamel, peas and ham, breaded and deep-fried into a crisp puck. Invented for leftovers, now sold at every fry shop and pizzeria counter. Eat it standing, before it cools and turns solid.

Beef and an enormous quantity of onions cooked down for hours into a sweet, brown, almost jam-like sauce for thick ziti. Despite the name it is entirely Neapolitan, and nobody in Genoa has heard of it. Ask for extra black pepper.

Pizza dough stuffed with ricotta, pork cracklings and tomato, sealed and deep-fried into a puffed golden pillow. Postwar food from years when ovens and money were both scarce. Cheaper than baked pizza and, on a cold day, better.

Small clams opened in olive oil, garlic and white wine, tossed with spaghetti and their own briny liquid, parsley over the top, cheese never. Ask for it with veraci, the tiny local clams, and use bread on the plate afterward.

Made from water buffalo milk in the flatlands north of the city and sold the day it is made, still warm at the best counters. Torn open, it should weep whey. Nothing like the rubbery blocks sold abroad under the same name.

Pasta and potatoes cooked in one pot until the starch turns it thick and almost gluey, with smoked provola stirred in at the end so it pulls into strings. Poverty cooking, and the dish Neapolitans actually crave when away.

Fried eggplant layered with tomato, basil and cheese and baked until the edges caramelize. Three regions claim to have invented it and the argument is unresolved. Best at room temperature the next day, which is how families serve it.

A tall mushroom of yeasted cake soaked in rum syrup until it is heavy and dripping. Brought south by French cooks at the Bourbon court and adopted completely. A good one is saturated rather than soggy, and needs no cream.

A lattice-topped tart of ricotta and cooked wheat berries scented with orange flower water, made for Easter and eaten for days afterward. The wheat is the point: a spring symbol far older than the holiday it now belongs to.

Espresso pulled short and strong, and sweetened before it reaches you unless you say otherwise, drunk standing at the bar in one swallow. Ask about the caffè sospeso — the habit of paying for a second cup a stranger can claim.

A fat pork sausage shot through with molten cheese, split and handed over at sidewalk stands with mustard, a bread roll and grated horseradish. The affectionate Viennese nickname translates as the pus-filled one. This is what the city eats at 2 a.m.

Clear beef broth with thin pancakes sliced into ribbons and dropped in at the last moment, so they soften without falling apart. The cheapest honest lunch in any Beisl, the wood-paneled neighborhood taverns where Vienna actually eats.

Sirloin under a heap of crisp fried onions in dark gravy loosened with beer, fried potatoes alongside. A tavern standard since the 1800s, when onions were how you made a small piece of beef feed a whole table. Ask for it medium at most.

Beef simmered until a spoon goes through it, brought to the table in its own copper pot of broth with apple-horseradish and a chive sauce. Emperor Franz Joseph ate it nearly every day for 68 years. Drink the broth first, then eat the meat.

Squares of egg pasta tossed with cabbage cooked slowly in sugar and pork fat until it caramelizes almost black at the edges. Poor-kitchen cooking that stayed on menus because it tastes far better than it sounds. Pepper it heavily. A winter dish.

A wooden board of cured pork, blood sausage, pickles, black bread and Liptauer, a paprika-spiked cheese spread. This is the food of a Heuriger, the taverns on the city edge where wine growers pour their own vintage. Order a spritzer and stay.

Paella made with short toasted noodles instead of rice, cooked in fish stock until the ends stand upright and the bottom catches. From the fishing towns down the coast. Comes with garlic aioli to stir through at the table.

Fish and potatoes stewed in broth thickened with ground almonds and garlic, built from whatever the boats brought in. Fishermen cooked it on board with the fish they could not sell. Ask for bread; the broth is the point.

Pasta tubes filled with the roast meat left over from the day before, covered in béchamel and baked until the top browns. Catalans eat them on December 26th, which is when the leftovers exist. An import that became a ritual.

Long sweet spring onions charred black over vine cuttings, peeled at the table and dipped in romesco, a red sauce of almonds and peppers. Eaten in a bib, with your hands. January to March only, and worth planning around.

A flat sweet bread strewn with candied fruit and pine nuts, eaten on the night of June 23rd with cava and fireworks on the beach. Sold everywhere for one week and nowhere the rest of the year. Buy it the day you see it.

Marzipan balls rolled in pine nuts and baked until the nuts toast, made for All Saints on November 1st and eaten with sweet wine. Almond-dense and slightly chewy. Bakeries pile them in the windows for a fortnight, then stop.

Custard set with cornstarch rather than cream, scented with lemon peel and cinnamon, sugar burned to glass on top with a hot iron. Lighter than crème brûlée and older — Catalan cookbooks describe it in the 1300s.

A chickpea and meat stew served in three courses from one pot: the broth first as a noodle soup, then the chickpeas and vegetables, then the meats. Winter food that takes all morning to make. Order it before two or it is gone.

Rings of squid in a light batter stuffed into a crusty roll with nothing else — no sauce, no salad, just squid and bread. Madrid sits two hundred miles from the sea and eats this anyway. A lemon wedge, if you insist.

Potatoes cooked slowly in olive oil until soft, bound with egg and set into a thick cake that should stay runny at the center. The argument about adding onion is real and unresolved. Eaten hot, cold, in a sandwich, at any hour.

Potato, tuna, egg and vegetables bound in mayonnaise, served cold in a mound with breadsticks stuck in it. It sounds like a picnic salad and tastes far better, and every bar in the city is quietly judged on its version.

Béchamel cooked with cured ham until stiff enough to shape, breaded and fried so the crust cracks and the inside runs. It is supposed to be molten. Homemade ones are lumpy and uneven, which is how you know they are homemade.

Fried eggs broken over fried potatoes and usually ham, then stirred together at the table until the yolk coats everything. Nothing about it is refined. It is what Madrid eats at midnight, and again the next morning.

Shrimp cooked in a clay dish of olive oil with sliced garlic and dried chili, brought to the table still bubbling. The oil is the actual reason to order it. Ask for bread first — it will be gone before the shrimp are.

Day-old bread simmered in broth with garlic and paprika until it collapses, an egg cracked in at the end to poach in the heat. Hard-times food that outlived the hard times. Winter only, in a tavern with tiles on the walls.

Ham from black-footed pigs fattened on acorns in the oak pastures west of the city, cured for years and hand-sliced into sheets you can see through. The fat should melt on contact. Ask for bellota, and eat it at room temperature.

Spinach and chickpeas stewed with cumin, paprika and garlic-rubbed fried bread that dissolves and thickens the whole thing. A Lenten dish with Moorish bones, now eaten year-round. Order it as a tapa, with dark bread.

A small warm roll pressed around pringá: the pork, chorizo and blood sausage left at the end of a stew, mashed to a paste. Two bites, and deeply savory. What Seville eats standing at the bar at 2 a.m., and again at noon.

Pork cheeks braised in sherry and stock for hours until they give way completely, in a dark reduced sauce with fried potatoes. A cheap cut and a slow method — the most reliable thing on a Sevillian menu in winter.

Small snails simmered in a broth of cumin, mint and hot pepper, served in a bowl with a toothpick, the broth drunk afterward. Signs go up in April and come down by June. Lighter and more herbal than the Portuguese version.

Pork tenderloin in a sauce of garlic, lemon and whisky cooked down to a sharp brown glaze, over fried potatoes. A 1970s bar invention with no pedigree whatsoever, and possibly the most-ordered dish in the city.

Eggs baked in an earthenware dish over tomato, peppers, peas and ham until the whites just set and the yolks stay loose. A whole meal in one clay bowl. Break the yolks and eat it with bread, straight from the dish.

Wine-and-anise dough fried and then glazed in honey until sticky, dense and faintly perfumed. Made for both Christmas and Easter, by convents and grandmothers. They keep for weeks and improve over the first few days.

Egg yolks cooked with sugar syrup into small bright rounds, made by cloistered nuns and sold through a turntable so buyer and seller never meet. Sherry makers used the whites to clarify wine and gave the convents the yolks.

Crumbly shortbread of flour, lard and almonds that collapses to dust the moment you bite it — the name comes from the word for powder. Made in Andalusian towns for Christmas, wrapped in twists of paper. December, in practice.

Bone-dry sherry aged under a veil of live yeast in seaside cellars, tasting of salt and almonds and nothing sweet at all. Served cold in a small glass alongside anything fried. Ask by name; expect it to cost less than wine.

Pecorino and cracked black pepper whisked with starchy pasta water into a sauce that clings — no butter, no cream, and it seizes if you rush it. Three ingredients and the hardest plate in Rome to make well. Eat it the moment it lands.

A ball of tomato-stained rice with a plug of mozzarella at the center, breaded and deep-fried. Pull it apart and the cheese stretches like an old telephone cord, which is where the nickname came from. Eaten standing at a pizza counter.

Rectangular pizza baked in long trays, cut with scissors and sold by weight rather than the slice — point at what you want and say how much. The Roman base is thin and crisp, unlike Naples, and that argument is permanent.

Cured pork jowl, tomato, pecorino and chili on bucatini, the hollow spaghetti that sprays sauce when you bite it. It comes from a hill town east of the city. Take the tomato away and you have gricia, its older ancestor.

A whole artichoke pressed flat and fried twice, until the outer leaves turn to crisp petals and the heart stays soft. From the Roman Jewish quarter, cooked there for five centuries. February to April, when the artichokes arrive.

Chicory stems cut into curls and soaked in ice water until they twist, then dressed with anchovy, garlic and vinegar. Bitter, cold and sharp. A winter salad the rest of Italy barely makes. Ask whether they are in season yet.

Thin veal layered with prosciutto and a sage leaf, pinned together and cooked fast in butter and white wine. The name means jumps in the mouth. Four ingredients, six minutes, and no substitution worth making.

Oxtail stewed for hours with celery and tomato — and, in the old recipes, a little cocoa and raisin — until the meat gives up entirely. Cooked by slaughterhouse workers paid in the cuts nobody would buy. Order nothing after it.

A whole pig boned, packed with rosemary, garlic and fennel, rolled and roasted until the skin turns to glass. Sliced cold into a plain roll at market stalls. It belongs to the hill towns south of Rome and arrives by van.

Tripe simmered in tomato with mint and a heavy dusting of pecorino. Saturday was traditionally the day for it. Organ meat, entirely unashamed — and the mint is what keeps the whole thing from turning heavy.

A soft, faintly sweet bun split open and packed with an unreasonable quantity of unsweetened whipped cream. Eaten for breakfast alongside coffee, not as a dessert. Bakeries fill them in the morning and sell out by lunch.

Ice shaved by hand from a block, drowned in fruit syrup and topped with fresh fruit, sold from riverside kiosks that only open when the heat arrives. Older than the freezer. June through September, along the Tiber.

A T-bone three fingers thick from local Chianina cattle, seared over coals and served rare in the middle, no exceptions entertained. Priced by weight and meant for two or three people. Salt and olive oil, nothing else.

Chicken livers cooked down with capers, anchovy and sweet wine into a coarse dark paste spread on toast. It begins nearly every Tuscan meal. Stronger and far less sweet than a French pâté, and better with the local red.

Bread, white beans and black kale cooked into a thick mass, cooled, then cooked again — the name means reboiled, and that second cooking is the entire point. Winter only. It should be stiff enough to eat with a fork.

Small balls of fried bread dough served hot with stracchino, a soft young cheese, and prosciutto draped over the top. You build each bite yourself. They arrive with the wine and vanish before the menu is decided.

Stale bread simmered with tomato, garlic and basil until it collapses into a thick porridge, finished with raw olive oil poured over. Thrift turned into something people order on purpose. Warm, or room temperature in summer.

Wide ribbons of egg pasta under wild boar slow-cooked in red wine with juniper and rosemary until it shreds. The boar are hunted in the hills around the city, where they are a genuine nuisance. Autumn and winter food.

Beef shin stewed in Chianti with a startling quantity of whole peppercorns and whole garlic cloves. Kiln workers cooked it beside the tiles they were firing for the cathedral dome. No stock and no vegetables — wine and pepper.

Stale bread soaked and squeezed dry, then torn up with tomato, cucumber, onion and basil and dressed with oil and vinegar. A summer salad built on bread that would otherwise be thrown away. Only as good as the tomatoes.

Hard almond biscuits baked twice, with a small glass of sweet amber wine to dunk them in until they soften. The wine ages in attic barrels through the temperature swings of the seasons. This is how a Tuscan meal ends.

Haddock salted, tied in pairs and hot-smoked over hardwood in a barrel until the skin blackens and the flesh cooks through. Protected by law and made only near one Angus town. Eat it warm from the paper, with butter.

Sausage meat pressed into a loaf and sliced into squares, so that it fits a square roll exactly — which is the reason it exists. Fried for breakfast and eaten in a morning roll with brown sauce. Nobody else makes it.

Toasted oats, raspberries, cream and honey folded together with a slug of whisky and served in a glass. Traditionally a harvest dish. The oats must be toasted and the raspberries Scottish, which is worth the fuss in July.

Sugar, condensed milk and butter boiled and beaten until it sets into a crumbly, grainy block that dissolves rather than chews. Sweeter and harder than fudge. Sold at church sales and school fairs, in slabs, by weight.

A pancake made from both grated raw and mashed cooked potato, fried on a griddle until crisp outside and dense within. An old rhyme says a woman who cannot make it will never marry. Served rolled around meat, or at breakfast.

Mashed potato beaten with kale or cabbage and scallions, with a well of melted butter in the middle. Eaten at Halloween with charms hidden inside to tell fortunes. The butter is not a garnish — it is the reason to eat it.

A dark tea-soaked fruit loaf, sliced and buttered, with a ring baked inside at Halloween — whoever finds it is said to marry within the year. The name comes from the Irish for speckled bread. Sold all year, eaten in autumn.

An open sandwich on dense rye built in a fixed order: butter, then one topping — pickled herring, roast pork, breaded plaice, shrimp — then garnish. Eaten with a knife and fork at lunch. Never stacked, never picked up.

A red sausage in a bun, roasted rather than boiled, under remoulade, ketchup, mustard, both raw and crisp fried onions, and pickled cucumber. Sold from a pølsevogn, the sausage wagons that have stood on Danish streets since 1921.

Pan-fried pork and veal meatballs, flattened slightly by the spoon that shapes them, with potatoes and pickled beetroot — or cold in a sandwich the next day. Every Danish family claims a different ratio of pork to veal.

Thick slices of pork belly fried until the fat crisps, with boiled potatoes and a parsley cream sauce poured over everything. Voted the national dish by public ballot in 2014. Some places serve it until you surrender.

Herring cured in vinegar with onion, bay and peppercorn, laid on buttered rye. Sharp, oily and nothing like the tinned kind. The traditional order is herring first at lunch, and always with a cold shot alongside.

Dense sour rye packed with whole grains and seeds, dark enough to look black and heavy enough to work as a plate. Danes eat it daily and judge it seriously. Everything else in a Danish lunch is sitting on top of it.

Small crisp pastry shells filled with chicken and asparagus in white sauce, served two to a plate. Deeply unfashionable, quietly beloved, and served at family gatherings without irony. A dish that peaked in 1960 and stayed.

A thick beef patty fried and served under a heap of soft browned onions, with gravy, potatoes and pickles. Not a burger — there is no bun, and the onions are the point. Danish lunchtime cooking at its plainest and best.

Pork roasted with the rind scored into strips so it blisters into crackling you can snap. Hot at Christmas with red cabbage, and cold the rest of the year on rye with pickled cucumber. The crackling is the entire event.

Spherical pancakes cooked in a cast-iron pan of round wells, turned with a knitting needle until they close into balls, then dusted with sugar and dipped in jam. Christmas market food, eaten with mulled wine from a paper tray.

Cold buttermilk whisked with egg, sugar, vanilla and lemon into a thin sweet soup, with small dry biscuits floated on top. Sold in cartons from May and eaten as lunch on hot days. Strange the first time and then not at all.

Stewed red summer berries thickened into a loose pudding and poured with cream. It is also the sentence Danes ask foreigners to pronounce, because the vowels are impossible. Order it and let them enjoy watching.

A soft vanilla sponge under coconut and brown sugar baked in butter until it caramelizes into a crackling crust. The name means dream cake. It came out of a village baking contest in the 1960s and never left.

Clear caraway or dill spirit served ice cold in a tiny glass beside herring, drunk in one swallow with a nod down the table. Not sipped and never mixed. One with the herring, one with the cheese, and then stop.

Small pork and beef meatballs with cream gravy, boiled potatoes, lingonberry jam and pickled cucumber. The lingonberry is not a garnish — its sourness is what the gravy is built against. Thursday and Sunday food.

A mound of hand-peeled shrimp on buttered bread with egg, dill and mayonnaise, piled until the bread disappears. Ordered as a light lunch, though nothing about it is light. Judge it on whether the shrimp were peeled by hand.

Small Baltic herring floured and fried in butter, with mashed potato, lingonberry and raw onion, often from a harbor stall. Softer and sweeter than sea herring. Eat it standing on the quay in the cold, out of paper.

Yellow pea soup with pork and mustard, followed by thin pancakes with jam and cream — soup then dessert, in that order, on Thursdays. The habit comes from old fasting rules and outlived the reason entirely.

A thick, mild smoked sausage of beef and pork, sliced and fried or baked whole with mustard. Its recipe is protected by law. It came from a mining town where ox hides were made into rope and the meat had to go somewhere.

Shrimp folded with mayonnaise, dill and a little roe on fried bread, invented by a restaurateur on a boat in 1956 and named for a Danish cape. It became the standard Swedish starter and has not moved since.

A sandwich built like a layer cake — bread layered with shrimp, egg, ham or salmon, the outside frosted in cream cheese and decorated. Served at birthdays and funerals. It looks like a joke and is taken entirely seriously.

Potato, onion and cured sprats layered with cream and baked until the top browns and the fish dissolves into it. The sprats are cured with sugar and spice, so it turns sweet and salty at once. A Christmas table fixture.

A cardamom bun hollowed out, filled with almond paste and whipped cream and capped with its own lid. Sold between Christmas and Easter, and once eaten only on the Tuesday before Lent. A Swedish king died after eating too many.

Cardamom dough rolled with cinnamon butter, knotted rather than spiraled, topped with pearl sugar. The centerpiece of fika, the coffee break Swedes take seriously enough to schedule. It has an official day, October 4th.

Sponge, jam, vanilla custard and a dome of whipped cream sealed under bright green marzipan with a pink rose on top. Created for three Swedish princesses in the 1930s. Unchanging, everywhere, and better than it needs to be.

A sweet spiced arrack liqueur Sweden drank obsessively for two centuries, served warm alongside Thursday pea soup or cold after dinner. Nearly forgotten, then revived. Sweeter than you expect and stronger than it tastes.

A flat chocolate cake deliberately underbaked so the middle stays sticky, served with cream. The name means sticky cake. Every Swede can make it from memory and it takes about ten minutes to put together.

Large beef patties, coarser and heavier than meatballs, in brown gravy with mashed peas, potatoes and lingonberry. The everyday dinner Norwegians grow up on and order as adults when they want looking after.

Mutton on the bone and cabbage layered in a pot with whole peppercorns and boiled for hours, with nothing else added at all. Voted the national dish twice. Eaten every autumn, and it has its own Thursday in late September.

Dense dumplings of grated raw and cooked potato, boiled and served with salted meat, sausage and rutabaga. They go by a different name in nearly every valley. Thursday is the day, and the leftovers get fried next morning.

Cold-water shrimp boiled at sea and sold straight off the boat at the harbor, peeled by hand onto white bread with mayonnaise and lemon, with beer. A summer ritual more than a dish. Buy a kilo and take all afternoon.

Cream-based fish soup with root vegetables and whatever white fish came in, thickened lightly and finished with dill. Every coastal town has its version. The correct thing to eat when the weather is against you.

Salmon buried in salt, sugar and dill for a few days until it firms and cures without any smoke — the name means buried salmon, from when it was fermented in sand. Sliced thin, with sweet mustard sauce and dark bread.

Brown cheese made by boiling whey until the milk sugars caramelize, shaved into thin sheets with a slicer Norway invented. Sweet, fudgy and faintly goaty. Eaten on toast at breakfast and on waffles in the afternoon.

Trout salted and fermented in a barrel for months, then eaten raw with flatbread, sour cream and onion. Sharper and stranger than cured fish has any right to be. Autumn and winter, and a real test even for Norwegians.

Thick soft pancakes cooked on a griddle and folded around butter and brown cheese, or sour cream and jam. Sold on the coastal ferries, which is where most Norwegians eat them. Impossible to stop at one.

Cloudberries — amber, tart, and picked from bogs in locations people genuinely keep secret — folded through whipped cream with sugar. Served at Christmas. They cost what they cost because nobody can farm them properly.

Potato spirit flavored with caraway and dill and aged in oak, some of it shipped across the equator and back because the motion is said to improve it. Drunk cold with fatty food at Christmas, in small glasses, slowly.

A thin rye crust folded around rice porridge and baked until the edges char, brushed with butter and topped with chopped egg mashed into more butter. Eaten at breakfast, sold everywhere. From Karelia, on the eastern border.

Sour rye, dense and dark, traditionally baked in rings with a hole so it could hang from a pole to dry. Finns living abroad have it mailed to them. Eaten with butter and nothing else, and taken more seriously than any other food.

Salmon soup with potato, leek and cream, finished with a heavy hand of dill and butter melting on the surface. Served in the market halls with rye bread. The salmon should be in large soft pieces, never shredded.

Tiny lake vendace rolled in rye flour and fried whole — heads, bones and all — served in a paper cone with garlic mayonnaise and lemon. Market square food, eaten with your fingers, crisp and salty and gone in two minutes.

Reindeer shaved into thin curls, sautéed in butter and served with mashed potato and lingonberry. Lean and only faintly gamy, closer to beef than to venison. It comes from Lapland, where herding is Sámi work.

A flat cheese made from first-milking colostrum, baked until it blisters brown and squeaks against your teeth, served warm with cloudberry jam. The name means bread cheese. Always heated, never eaten cold.

Fat pork sausage grilled slowly until the skin splits, eaten with mustard and beer beside a lake or straight after a sauna. Not a delicacy and not pretending to be. The smell of Finnish summer, along with woodsmoke.

Rye flour and malt baked slowly into a dark, thick, faintly sweet pudding, eaten cold with cream and sugar at Easter. It looks alarming and tastes like malt bread. Finns are entirely aware of how it looks.

Sweet cardamom bread braided or knotted and scattered with pearl sugar, torn apart and eaten with coffee — and Finland drinks more coffee per person than anywhere on earth. The cardamom is heavy, and should be.

A cylindrical almond and rum cake topped with raspberry jam inside a ring of icing, eaten on February 5th for the national poet, and said to have been invented by his wife. Sold from January, gone by mid-February.

Semolina cooked with lingonberry and then whipped until it turns pale pink and foamy and doubles in size. Served cold with milk poured over it. A dessert made of porridge, and far better than that sounds.

Salty licorice, black and hard, flavored with ammonium chloride — actually salty rather than sweet. Finns eat it constantly and put it in ice cream and vodka. Most foreign visitors do not recover from the first piece.

Lightly fermented lemon and brown sugar mead, made at home in bottles with a few raisins that float to the top when it is ready. Drunk at May Day with sugared doughnuts, in the first warm week of the year.

Veal meatballs poached and served in a white sauce made sharp with capers and lemon, over potatoes or rice. Named for a Prussian city that is now Russian. East Berlin canteens kept the dish alive for decades.

A cured pork knuckle boiled until the meat slides off the bone and the fat turns to jelly, with pea puree and sauerkraut. Boiled rather than roasted, which surprises anyone expecting crackling. Enormous, and cheap for the size.

A sour, smoky soup of pickled cucumber, sausage, tomato and lemon, borrowed from Soviet kitchens and made East German. Sharp enough to wake you up. Still on older menus here and almost unknown further west.

Boiled potatoes sliced and fried hard with bacon and onion until the edges caramelize, usually under a fried egg. A side dish everyone orders as a meal. The potatoes must be boiled the day before or they fall apart.

The Berlin bread roll — crisp-crusted, split down the middle, and the base of most breakfasts here. Nothing about it is remarkable except that Berliners insist it is, and that the word is used in this city and nowhere else.

Cocoa and coconut fat poured over layers of plain biscuits and chilled into a dark dense loaf that gets sliced like cake. No baking at any point. A childhood birthday standard on both sides of the wall.

White asparagus grown under mounded soil so it never sees light, peeled and boiled and served with hollandaise, ham and potatoes. For eight weeks each spring it takes over every menu in the city, then disappears completely.

Beef sirloin braised with root vegetables, the vegetables blended into a thick cream sauce, served with bread dumplings, a spoon of cranberry and a curl of whipped cream. Sweet, sour and rich at once. The Sunday dish.

Roast pork, bread dumplings and stewed sauerkraut — three words always said together, and the national dish. The dumplings exist to mop up the fat and the cabbage exists to cut through it. Order it once, early.

Beef stewed dark with onion, paprika and usually dark beer, served with bread dumplings and raw onion scattered on top. Thicker than the Hungarian soup and served differently from the Viennese. The beer in the sauce is the tell.

A slab of Edam breaded and deep-fried, with fries and tartar sauce. Invented for meat-free days under socialism and now the standard thing to eat at 2 a.m. Nobody claims it is good for you and everybody eats it.

A thin potato pancake with garlic, marjoram and a little flour, fried crisp and handed over on a paper plate at markets, sometimes wrapped around smoked meat. The marjoram is what makes it Czech and not a hash brown.

A fat sausage pickled in vinegar with onion, chili and bay for weeks until it turns sour and soft. The name means drowned man. Sold from jars kept on the bar in old pubs, eaten with dark bread and beer and nothing else.

A creamy dill soup with potato, wild mushrooms, vinegar and a poached egg dropped in at the end. Sour and herbal and unlike anything else on the table. The best argument against the idea that Czech food is all brown.

A whole soft white cheese marinated in oil with garlic, peppercorns and chili until it turns pungent and spreadable. Pub food, served with bread. It improves the longer it sits in the jar, up to a point.

Open sandwiches built on a slice of white bread with potato salad as the base, then ham, egg, salami or fish arranged neatly on top. Sold by the piece from delicatessen counters. A party food that became an everyday one.

Garlic soup with potato, croutons and often cheese, made with a quantity of garlic that would be a mistake anywhere else. Ordered for hangovers and colds. It is medicine that happens to taste extremely good.

A round yeast pastry with a well of poppy seed, plum or curd cheese in the middle, baked soft. Made by the hundred for weddings, which is where the name comes from. Best from a bakery while still slightly warm.

Head cheese — meat set in its own jelly — sliced and served with raw onion and a great deal of vinegar. Pub food from an era when nothing was thrown away. Cold, sharp and gelatinous, and better with beer than it sounds.

A braided ring of dough boiled and then baked, sold from blue carts on every corner with salt, poppy or sesame. Kraków has made them since the 1300s and they are protected by EU law. Buy one early; they stale by noon.

A halved baguette loaded with mushrooms and cheese, grilled until it bubbles, then finished with a stripe of ketchup and whatever else you point at. Sold from the round hall in the old Jewish quarter until very late.

Sour rye soup, fermented for days, with white sausage, potato and half a boiled egg, sometimes served inside a hollowed loaf. Sour in a way no other soup is. Eaten at Easter, and available here all year round.

Clear beetroot broth, deep red and sharpened with lemon and a little sugar, served as a soup or drunk from a cup in winter. At Christmas it arrives with small mushroom dumplings floating in it. Nothing like a heavy borscht.

Sausage grilled over wood in the back of a blue van that parks by the river at night and drives off at dawn. Served on a paper plate with a roll and mustard. It has run for decades, and the line is part of it.

Tripe cut into ribbons and simmered for hours with root vegetables and marjoram into a thick, peppery soup. Sold in bars as a hangover cure and at weddings at two in the morning. Organ meat, but mild — the marjoram carries it.

Baked curd cheesecake under a shortcrust lattice, denser and far less sweet than the American kind, often with raisins or candied orange. The Kraków version is defined by that pastry lattice across the top.

Apple cake with a thick layer of grated spiced apple between shortcrust, served warm with cream. Every café makes one and every one disagrees about how much cinnamon is acceptable. Order it with tea in the afternoon.

A round doughnut filled with rose petal jam and glazed, eaten in enormous quantity on the Thursday before Lent — bakeries sell millions in a day and the lines run down the block. Rose is the traditional filling.

Drunk cold, neat, in one swallow, never sipped and never mixed, with food or a pickle immediately after. Poland argues with Russia about who invented it. Ordered by the small glass, with a toast before each one.

Beef cured with salt and mountain herbs, air-dried for months in the thin air of the eastern valleys, pressed into a dense rectangle and sliced tissue-thin. Deep red, intensely beefy, served with nothing at all.

Rolled oats soaked overnight in milk with grated apple, lemon and nuts, invented around 1900 by a Zurich doctor for his patients. The original is far wetter and much less sweet than the packaged version it inspired.

A braided butter and milk bread with a glossy egg-washed crust, baked for Sunday breakfast across the country. Soft, faintly sweet, and torn rather than sliced. Bakeries sell out early on weekend mornings.

Small, feather-light macarons made by a Zurich confectioner since the 1950s — lighter and smaller than the Paris kind, sold by weight in pastel rows. They keep for two days at most, which is precisely the point.

Thin, hard honey biscuits stamped with detailed scenes from carved wooden molds, baked so fast that one side scorches while the other stays pale. A Zurich Christmas item made here since the 1400s. More carving than cookie.

A ring of bread dipped in grape molasses and crusted in sesame, sold from red carts on every corner and from men carrying trays on their heads. Chewy and faintly bitter. Eaten for breakfast, with tea, standing up.

A grilled mackerel fillet stuffed into half a loaf with raw onion, lettuce and lemon, sold from boats and stalls at the Galata bridge. Simple to the point of being nothing, and one of the best things in the city.
