Mussels stuffed with spiced rice, steamed and sold from trays on the street, opened one at a time and handed over with lemon. You pay by how many shells pile up. A late-night thing, and eaten in quantity.

A very thin round of dough spread with minced lamb, tomato and pepper and baked in seconds. Not a pizza — it is rolled around parsley and lemon and eaten by hand. Cheap enough to order two without thinking.
A boat of dough baked with cheese, egg or minced meat, the edges folded to hold the filling, cut into pieces with a rocking blade. Order it with kaşar cheese and a raw egg cracked into the middle.

Hand-minced lamb pressed onto a wide flat skewer and grilled over charcoal, spiced with red pepper and served with grilled tomato, onion and flatbread that soaks up the fat. Named for the southern city, and properly hot.

Tiny dumplings of spiced lamb, boiled and served under garlic yogurt with melted butter and dried mint and red pepper poured over. Small enough that forty fit on a spoon. The smaller they are, the better the cook.

Eggs scrambled slowly into tomato, green pepper and onion until soft and loose, served in the pan with bread for scooping. Breakfast, and the subject of one permanent national argument about whether onion belongs in it.

A large baked potato split and mashed in its skin with butter and cheese, then loaded with whatever you point at — olives, corn, sausage, pickles, russian salad. From Ortaköy, and the toppings are the entire event.

Lamb intestines wrapped around offal, grilled on a spit for hours, then chopped fine with oregano and pepper and stuffed into bread. Organ meat, and the thing Istanbul eats at 3 a.m. It smells better than it sounds.

Shredded pastry layered around unsalted stretchy cheese, baked in syrup and served hot so the cheese pulls when you cut it. Sweet and salty at once, topped with pistachio. Order it the moment it is made, never reheated.

Ice cream thickened with mastic and wild orchid root, so it stretches, resists the spoon and melts slowly. Vendors make a performance of taking it away from you before handing it over. Chewy in a way ice cream should not be.

Finely ground coffee simmered with sugar in a small pot and poured grounds and all, drunk in small sips until you reach the sludge. Ordered by sweetness, not size. Served with water and, if you are lucky, a fortune read after.

Small fingers of minced beef and lamb grilled over charcoal and served in a soft flatbread with raw onion and kajmak, by the five or the ten. The Balkans argue endlessly about whose are best. Ordered by number, not by plate.

Coiled phyllo filled with meat, cheese or spinach, baked in a huge round pan and sold by weight, cut in wedges. Eaten for breakfast with yogurt to drink. Greasy in a way that is the point rather than a flaw.

Red peppers roasted, peeled and cooked down with eggplant and oil into a thick relish, made in enormous batches every autumn and jarred for winter. Every family insists theirs is correct. Eaten on bread with cheese.

A fresh dairy spread skimmed from scalded milk and left to ripen, somewhere between clotted cream and young cheese, salty and slightly sour. Put on bread, on meat, inside everything. Nothing else quite tastes like it.

Layers of phyllo torn and mixed with eggs and salty white cheese, baked until the top curls and browns and the middle stays custardy. Served warm at every celebration and every ordinary breakfast alike.

Tomato, cucumber, onion and pepper under a heavy snow of grated white cheese. Named for a region straddling three borders, and claimed by all of them. The cheese should completely hide what is underneath.

A peppery freshwater fish soup, red with paprika, made from whatever the Danube and Sava gave up — carp, catfish, perch. Cooked in a kettle by the river. There is also a famous rock band named after it.

White beans slow-cooked with smoked ribs, paprika and bay until the broth thickens by itself. The everyday winter meal of the whole country, cooked in vast pots. Eaten with raw onion and bread, and better reheated.

A fierce spread of crumbled white cheese, garlic, hot paprika and oil, mashed into a rough paste — the name translates roughly as chaos or pandemonium. Served with grilled meat, and it will overpower anything near it.

Two thin layers of pastry with several centimeters of set vanilla custard between them, cut into squares and dusted with sugar. Sold from bakery windows in a solid slab. Eat it with a fork; it does not survive being picked up.

Ridged batter piped into hot oil, fried until deep gold and then soaked in cold sugar syrup so it stays crisp outside and syrupy within. Sold from trays, by the piece. Ottoman by inheritance, and sweeter than it looks.

Fruit brandy — plum most often, but quince, apricot and pear all exist — distilled at home in enormous quantity. Drunk before a meal rather than after, at room temperature, in small glasses. Everyone claims an uncle who makes it.

Skinless grilled sausages of beef and lamb with garlic, pepper and baking soda, which is what makes them springy. Served in a pile with mustard and bread, never a bun. Ordered by the piece and eaten with beer, outdoors.

Cabbage leaves — pickled, not fresh — rolled around pork and rice with dill, cooked slowly with smoked meat and served with polenta and sour cream. Smaller and sourer than the Hungarian version. Christmas, and every Sunday.

Cornmeal cooked to a thick polenta and turned out in a mound, cut with a thread rather than a knife. Eaten with cheese, sour cream, or under stew. It replaced bread for centuries in the countryside, and often still does.

Tripe soup, white with sour cream and egg yolk, sharpened with vinegar and garlic and served scaldingly hot. The national hangover cure. Order it with a small dish of hot peppers and use them, one bite at a time.

Meatball soup soured with fermented wheat bran, thick with vegetables and finished with lovage — an herb that tastes like celery multiplied. The sourness is the defining feature of Romanian soup, and it takes a moment.

Eggplant roasted over flame until the skin burns, then chopped with oil and onion into a smoky, loose paste — never blended smooth. Served cold with tomato on bread. The wood-smoke taste is the whole reason for it.

Soft bread rings crusted in salt, poppy or sesame, sold hot from windows in the street for small change. Closer to a soft pretzel than a bagel. Eaten walking, at any hour, and best from a window with a line.

A baked loaf of chopped lamb offal with herbs, egg and onion, wrapped in caul fat and served cold in slices at Easter. Somewhere between a terrine and a meatloaf. Organ meat, and much gentler than the description.

Thin pastry folded around salty cheese, potato, cabbage or apple and pan-fried or baked. Sold from bakeries and roadside stands in a paper napkin. The savory cheese one, eaten hot, is the one to start with.

Two fried curd cheese doughnuts, one large with a small one perched on top, buried in sour cream and sour cherry jam. Enormous, hot, and meant to be shared, though nobody actually does. Order it after almost nothing else.

A sweet braided loaf swirled with ground walnuts, cocoa and rum, baked for Easter and Christmas and eaten in thick slices for days after. Dense, faintly boozy, and better toasted once it is a day or two old.

Plum spirit, drunk cold in a small glass before food rather than after, and usually made at home rather than bought. Stronger than it tastes going down. Refusing a second is understood; refusing the first is not.
Ham and butter in a baguette and nothing else: no cheese, no salad, no mustard unless you ask. France eats over a billion a year. The whole thing rests on the bread and the butter being good.

Snails baked in their shells under garlic, parsley and a great deal of butter, served in a dimpled dish with tongs and a narrow fork. The snail is a delivery system for the butter, and the bread finishes the job.

Veal poached gently with carrot and onion, the broth turned into a cream sauce with egg yolk and lemon. Nothing is browned at any stage, which is the actual definition. Served with rice, and quietly loved by everyone.

A sausage made from coarsely cut pig intestine, grilled and served with mustard. It smells strongly of what it is, and you will either find it magnificent or you will not. Look for the AAAAA mark; the association is real.

Oysters from Brittany and Normandy, eaten raw by the half dozen with rye bread, butter and lemon, in brasseries with a shellfish stall out front. Ask for the flat ones if you want the strong metallic kind.

Chickpea flour cooked to a paste, set, cut into batons and fried until crisp outside and creamy within, then salted hard. Sold from stalls in the old fishing quarter. The local answer to a french fry, and older.

A ring of choux pastry split and filled with praline cream, created in 1910 to mark a bicycle race and shaped like a wheel. Hazelnut-heavy and less sweet than it looks. Eaten with a fork, never with hands.

Garlic pounded with olive oil into a stiff yellow mayonnaise, served with poached salt cod, boiled vegetables and eggs — a whole Friday meal named after its sauce. The garlic is fierce and is meant to be.

Summer vegetable and bean soup with a spoon of basil, garlic and oil stirred in at the table rather than cooked into it. Related to pesto, without pine nuts. Made when the beans are fresh, in late July and August.

Sheep tripe parcels stuffed with salt pork and garlic, tied by hand and braised with trotters in white wine and tomato for hours. Organ meat, slow and gelatinous, and a genuine local specialty. Order it at lunch.

Tiny whole cuttlefish floured and flash-fried, with lemon and sometimes garlic and parsley thrown over. Eaten with fingers at harbor tables. Sweeter and more tender than squid, and gone within minutes of arriving.

A long ridged doughnut fried to order and rolled in sugar, sold on the seafront and out at the beach villages. Orange-flower scented and greasy in the correct way. Eat it hot, from the paper, with your hands.
Hard, dry boat-shaped biscuits scented with orange flower, baked at the same bakery near the abbey since 1781 and blessed in February at Candlemas. Meant for dunking, and they keep for months.

Potatoes fried twice — once low to cook them, once hot to crisp them — in a paper cone from a friture, with a sauce chosen off a list of twenty. Belgium claims the invention and defends it. Mayonnaise, or ask for andalouse.

Mussels steamed with white wine, celery and onion, arriving in the black pot they cooked in with fries alongside. Use an empty shell as tongs for the rest. In season from summer into winter, cheapest in autumn.
Beef stewed in dark Belgian beer with onions, a slice of mustard-spread bread laid on top to dissolve and thicken it. Sweeter and deeper than a wine stew. Served with fries, because everything is.

Potatoes mashed roughly with a vegetable — carrot, leek, endive, kale — and a great deal of butter, served with sausage or bacon. Working-class Brussels food. The vegetable changes with the season and nobody minds.

Chicken or fish poached in broth with root vegetables and thickened with cream and egg yolk, landing between a soup and a stew. From Ghent, adopted here. Eaten with a spoon and a fork at the same time.

Belgian endive wrapped in ham, covered in béchamel and cheese and baked until browned. The endive stays faintly bitter under all of it, which is the point. It is grown in the dark, in cellars, near this city.

Raw beef minced with capers, onion, mustard and egg yolk, spread thickly on bread or served with fries. Nothing American about it. Sold in every butcher shop and eaten at lunch without any ceremony at all.

A light rectangular waffle with deep pockets, made from thin yeasted batter, crisp outside and hollow within, eaten warm with powdered sugar and nothing else. This is the one to eat with a knife and fork.

Large pork and beef meatballs in a dark sweet-sour sauce built on regional syrup, with fries. There is no rabbit involved — the name comes from the man who invented it. Sticky, strange, and better than it sounds.
A dense, chewy waffle made from bread dough studded with pearl sugar that caramelizes on the iron into a crackling crust. Uneven-edged, eaten hot from a stand, and nothing like the Brussels kind.

Thin, hard spiced biscuits pressed in carved wooden molds, tasting of cinnamon, clove and brown sugar, served with coffee everywhere. Belgium exported the crushed spread version, but the biscuit came first.

A cone-shaped sweet with a hard crust and thick raspberry syrup inside, sold from purple carts. It lasts about three weeks before the center crystallizes, which is why it never exported. Bite the tip and squeeze.

Veal lungs and heart cooked down with root vegetables into a fine sour ragout, sharpened with vinegar and capers and served with a bread dumpling. Organ meat, and the dish old Viennese cooking is proudest of. Order it where the menu is German only.

A thick pancake torn into pieces in the pan, caramelized in butter and sugar, buried under powdered sugar and served with stewed plums. Named for Emperor Franz Joseph. Austrians order it as a main course at lunch, and so should you.

Apples, raisins, cinnamon and buttered breadcrumbs rolled in pastry stretched so thin a baker is supposed to read a newspaper through it. The layering technique arrived with the Ottomans. Eat it warm, with vanilla sauce rather than cream.

Sweet yeast buns baked pressed together in one dish so they tear apart rather than slice, filled with plum jam and served warm under vanilla sauce. Coffeehouse food from the Czech half of the old empire. Best late, straight from the tray.

A whole apricot wrapped in potato dough, boiled, then rolled in buttered breadcrumbs and sugar. The fruit stays whole and bursts hot when you cut it. Made with apricots from the Wachau valley upriver, and only worth eating in July and August.

Espresso lengthened with hot milk and capped with foam, closer to a cappuccino than to anything American. It arrives on a silver tray with a glass of water, refilled as long as you sit. The coffeehouse habit itself is UNESCO-listed.
Two thin waffle discs with caramel syrup between them, cut fresh off the iron at markets. Rest it over a hot drink so the steam softens the syrup before you eat it. That instruction is not optional.

Potatoes mashed with kale, endive or sauerkraut, with a smoked sausage pressed into the middle and a well of gravy. Winter food, eaten early in the evening. Every version has a name and a devoted constituency.

Round versions of the same ragout, breaded and fried and served by the dozen with mustard beside beer. The standard order in a brown café at five in the afternoon. Wait two minutes or you will burn your mouth.

Chunks of cod in seasoned batter, deep-fried and served in a tray with garlic or tartar sauce from a market fish stall. Originally made from cheeks and offcuts. The best stalls fry to order and the line still moves fast.

A disc of yeasted dough deep-fried until it blisters, rubbed with garlic water and buried under sour cream and grated cheese. Market and beach food, sold from stands and eaten with both hands. Get it the moment it leaves the fryer.

A slab of bread spread with pork lard, showered with sweet paprika and topped with raw onion rings. Peasant food that the ruin bars kept alive as something to eat while drinking. Salty, rich, and completely convincing after the second beer.

Thin pancakes rolled around minced veal, laid in a paprika and sour cream sauce and baked. A savory starter that looks like dessert and confuses every first-time visitor. Named for the grass plains east of the city.

A thick vegetable stew — peas, lentils, squash, spinach — somewhere between a soup and a side, thickened with flour and sour cream. The everyday Hungarian lunch nobody puts on a postcard. Eaten with a fried egg or a sausage on top.

Cabbage leaves rolled around pork and rice, simmered for hours with sauerkraut and smoked meat, served under a spoon of sour cream. Better on the second day, which is why families make vats of it. Winter food that outlasts winter.

Roasted beef marrow bones served with toast, coarse salt and a narrow spoon for digging. Traditionally eaten alongside gulyás, spread thick on the bread. Rich to the point of absurdity — one bone is plenty, and markets serve it before noon.

Three kinds of sponge soaked in rum and layered with walnuts, chocolate sauce, raisins and whipped cream until it collapses into itself. A trifle with no structural ambition. Order it when you have already eaten too much.

Five thin sponge layers stacked with chocolate buttercream under a sheet of hard caramel that cracks when the fork goes in. Invented in 1885, when that caramel lid was a trick for keeping a cake fresh without refrigeration.

Crepes filled with ground walnuts, raisins and rum under dark chocolate sauce, flamed at the table. Created at the Gundel restaurant in 1894 and copied everywhere since. The walnut filling, not the fire, is the actual point.

Sweet dough wound around a spit and rolled in sugar that caramelizes over coals into a crackling shell, then unwound in a spiral as you eat it. Transylvanian by origin, sold at every market. Cinnamon is the only topping worth having.

A ring of bread crusted in sesame seeds, sold from street carts from before dawn and eaten on the way to work. Chewy, faintly sweet, and stale by afternoon, which is why vendors sell out and go home by noon.

Chilled sour cherry soup, thickened with sour cream and scented with clove and cinnamon, served as a first course rather than a dessert. Cold, pink and startling on a hot day. Summer only, while the cherries are in.

Semolina custard between sheets of phyllo, baked, then cut up with a scraper and dusted with sugar and cinnamon in front of you. There is a savory cheese version too. Breakfast, and best from a shop that makes nothing else.

Spinach, feta, dill and scallion between layers of oiled phyllo, baked until the top shatters. Sold in bakeries by the slab all day. The good ones have far more greens than cheese and are never soggy underneath.

Tomato, cucumber, onion, pepper, olives and a whole slab of feta with oregano and olive oil — the village salad, and no lettuce anywhere in it. The oil left in the bowl is meant to be finished with bread.

Yellow split peas cooked to a smooth puree, served warm with raw onion, capers, lemon and a pour of olive oil. Not made from fava beans, despite everything. The best comes from Santorini and is worth asking about.

A slab of hard cheese floured and fried in a small pan until it blisters and browns, served with lemon squeezed over it while it is still sizzling. Order it before the rest of the food and eat it immediately.

Large white beans baked slowly in tomato with dill and olive oil until they go creamy inside. Served warm or at room temperature as part of a mezze spread. Nothing about it is fast, and it is better the next day.

Small yeast doughnuts fried and drowned in honey syrup with cinnamon and walnuts, served hot by the dozen. Said to have been given to victors at the ancient games. Eat them fast, before the syrup soaks all the way in.

Semolina custard baked in phyllo and soaked in lemon syrup while still hot, so the top stays crisp and the base goes sticky. Cut into squares. Sweeter and more solid than it looks, and impossible to eat delicately.

Small oval cookies of olive oil, orange and semolina soaked in honey syrup and topped with crushed walnuts. Made at Christmas by the hundred. They keep for weeks, and the syrup gets deeper into them as they sit.

Spinach wilted in olive oil with pine nuts and raisins soaked until they plump, sometimes with a little cured ham. Sweet and savory at once, and a taste of the Moorish centuries still sitting on Catalan menus.

Eggplant, peppers and onions charred whole over flame until the skins blacken, then peeled, torn into strips and dressed with oil. The name comes from the Catalan for cooking in embers. Served cold, usually piled on bread.

Salt cod torn by hand — never cut — and served raw, cured only by its own salt, with tomato, onion, olives and oil. The name means shredded. A summer dish from before refrigeration, and still the coolest thing on the table.

Tubular pasta with cinnamon-spiced meat sauce under béchamel, baked and cut into squares. The cinnamon is what makes it Greek rather than Italian. Family food and taverna food, and always cut with a straight edge.

A fist-sized ball of mashed potato stuffed with spiced ground meat, breaded and fried, then hit with garlic aioli and a spicy red sauce. Invented in the Barceloneta docks in the 1950s. Order two; nobody has ever ordered one.

Instant coffee whipped with water, sugar and ice into a thick foam, served in a tall glass with a straw. Invented by accident at a trade fair in 1957. Ordered by sweetness, and drunk over an hour, never quickly.

Layers of eggplant, spiced lamb and potato under a thick béchamel, baked until the top sets and browns. The version everyone knows was standardized by a Greek chef trained in France in the 1920s. Better warm than hot.

Pork or chicken grilled on skewers and wrapped in pita with tomato, onion, tzatziki and — this is not negotiable — a handful of fries inside the wrap. The cheapest full meal in the city, eaten standing or walking.

A squat black bottle of herbal bitters, forty-odd herbs aged in oak, tasting of licorice and burnt orange. Made by the same Budapest family since 1790, apart from the decades they spent in exile with the recipe. Drink it cold, after dinner.

A deep-fried roll of thick beef ragout, breaded and hot enough to burn you, in a soft white bun with mustard. The bread does nothing but hold it. Sold from vending machine walls, which is genuinely the best way.

Fries with mayonnaise, spiced peanut sauce and raw onion piled on together — the name means war, for how it looks. The peanut sauce arrived through Indonesia and colonial history. Eaten with a small plastic fork.

Small spongy pancakes made with buckwheat and yeast, cooked in a dimpled pan and served under butter and powdered sugar by the dozen. Eaten hot at winter markets with a tiny fork. Lighter than pancakes should be.

A tall apple cake with thick pastry and a cinnamon-heavy filling, wedged with whipped cream and eaten with coffee in the afternoon. Denser and less sweet than the American pie, and ordered by the slab.

A dozen or more small Indonesian dishes served at once around rice — satay, rendang, sambals, pickles, fried banana. Invented by Dutch colonists to display the range of Javanese cooking. A meal that takes hours.

Chocolate sprinkles eaten on buttered bread at breakfast, by adults, entirely without embarrassment. The butter is what makes them stick. The supermarket aisle for this is longer than the one for cereal.

Deep-fried dough balls with raisins, buried in powdered sugar, sold from trailers that appear in December and vanish in January. Eaten outdoors at New Year in the cold. Better than a doughnut, and gone by the 2nd.

Cheese aged from a few weeks to several years, running from soft and mild to hard, crystalline and almost caramel. Ask for oud, the aged kind, and eat it with mustard. Market stalls will cut samples for you.

Dense chocolate cake with a seam of apricot jam under a hard chocolate glaze, invented in 1832 by a sixteen-year-old apprentice. The hotel and the bakery that both claim it fought a seven-year lawsuit over the name. Plain whipped cream is not optional.

A blend of young and old lambic beers fermented with wild yeast from the air of one valley, refermented in the bottle and sour enough to startle you. Served corked, like wine. Nothing else in beer tastes like it.

Anise spirit poured into a glass and cut with five parts cold water, which turns it cloudy yellow. Drunk slowly in the shade before lunch with a bowl of olives. Ordering it neat marks you out instantly.

Black olives, capers, anchovy and oil pounded into a coarse paste — the name comes from the Provençal word for caper, not for olive. Spread on toast before dinner. It should taste more of caper than you expect.

A fish stew of rockfish, saffron and fennel, served as two courses: the broth first with rouille and toast, the fish after. Fishermen made it from what they could not sell. The real thing is costly and ordered a day ahead.

White wine with a measure of blackcurrant liqueur, named for a Burgundy priest and mayor who served it constantly. Ordered before dinner at a café table in the late afternoon. Kir royal swaps the wine for champagne.
Three sheets of caramelized puff pastry with pastry cream between, glazed and marbled on top. It is built to shatter and collapse the moment you cut it, which makes eating one gracefully impossible.

Choux pastry piped long, filled with chocolate or coffee cream and glazed on top in the same flavor. The name means lightning, supposedly for how fast it goes. Judge a pâtisserie on whether the glaze is thin and clean.

Chickpea fritters in pita with eggplant, cabbage, hummus and hot sauce, sold in the Marais with a line down the street. Not French in origin and entirely Parisian in practice. Eaten walking, and dripping.

Raw beef chopped by hand and mixed with capers, shallot, mustard and egg yolk, either at the table or in the kitchen. Chopped, never ground — that texture is the whole difference. Order it with fries.

Ham and cheese toasted with béchamel and more cheese on top, browned under a grill. Add a fried egg and it becomes a croque madame. Café food since 1910, and the test of whether a café bothers with its kitchen.

Laminated dough folded with butter dozens of times and baked until it shatters. A straight one is made with real butter and a curved one usually is not — that is the convention, and it holds. Buy it before nine and eat it plain.

Forty or more sheets of pastry, clarified butter and pistachio, baked and soaked in syrup. Sold by weight and by cut — ask for şöbiyet or fıstıklı. Real ones shatter rather than squash, and the pistachios should be green.

A soft drink made from milk whey — genuinely — that tastes faintly of apple and nothing at all like dairy. The Swiss drink it constantly and it has never sold anywhere else. Try the red one before anyone explains it.

Half a wheel of cheese heated at the cut edge and scraped molten over boiled potatoes, with pickles and cured meat. It arrives in waves, one plate at a time, for as long as you keep asking. Also strictly a winter thing.

Melted cheese with white wine and garlic in a communal pot, with bread cubes on long forks. Winter only — the Swiss find eating it in summer genuinely strange. Losing your bread in the pot carries a forfeit.

Grated potato pressed into a pan and fried until a crust forms on both sides, then turned out like a cake. Eaten as a side, or under egg and cheese as a meal. The country is divided by a cultural line named after it.

Half-moon dumplings, boiled or fried, filled with curd cheese and potato, meat, mushroom and cabbage, or fruit in summer. Order ruskie — the potato and cheese ones — first. Served with fried onion and sour cream.

Pickled herring rolled around a pickle and onion, pinned with a stick and eaten cold — traditionally the morning after drinking, on the theory that it helps. Sharp and oily, and sold in jars in every supermarket.

Meat stacked and grilled on a vertical spit, carved into flatbread with salad, cabbage and garlic and chili sauces. Invented in Berlin in the 1970s by Turkish workers — not in Turkey. The city eats it at every hour.

A pork sausage fried, sliced, and drowned in curried tomato sauce, eaten with a small wooden fork and a bread roll. Invented in 1949 by a woman who got the ingredients from British soldiers. There is a museum and there are arguments.

Dried cod soaked in lye until it turns translucent and gelatinous, then baked and served with bacon, peas and potatoes. Eaten at Christmas out of tradition and stubbornness. Divisive at every table it arrives on.

Dry stout poured in two stages with a rest between, which is why it takes nearly two minutes. Roasted barley makes it bitter rather than sweet, and it is served cool rather than cold. It genuinely does taste different here.

Chips, shredded salt-and-chili chicken, fried peppers and onions tossed with spice mix and served in a paper bag. Invented in a Dublin Chinese takeaway around 2010 and now everywhere. The newest Irish national dish.

Salmon cured in salt and cold-smoked over oak or beech, sliced thin onto brown bread with lemon and pepper. Irish smokehouses cure it less sweetly than the Scottish style. Ask which smokehouse it came from; they will know.

Native flat oysters from the west coast, briny and faintly metallic, eaten raw with lemon and brown bread. The traditional pairing is with stout, which sounds wrong and is not. September to April, while the water is cold.

Langoustines from the Irish Sea, small and sweet, split and grilled with garlic butter or served cold with mayonnaise. Most of the catch is exported, which is why eating them here is worth doing on purpose.

A boiled joint of cured bacon with cabbage cooked in the same salty water and potatoes alongside, usually under parsley sauce. This is what corned beef and cabbage was before it emigrated to America and changed meat.

Lamb or mutton with potato, onion and carrot simmered in water alone — no stock, no browning, no wine. The plainness is the recipe. Barley thickens it in some kitchens, an argument you can start deliberately.

Bread leavened with baking soda and buttermilk rather than yeast, so it goes from bowl to oven in minutes. A cross is cut in the top to help it rise. Brown and dense or white and cakey; both want butter and salt.

Bacon, sausage, egg, tomato and both black and white pudding, with fried soda bread alongside. White pudding is the same as black without the blood. Tea is not optional, and it is served all day, everywhere.

Sausages and rashers of bacon simmered pale with potato and onion in their own stock, never browned. A Dublin dish and only a Dublin dish, built from whatever needed using up before Friday. Ugly, soft, and deeply comforting.

Single malt comes from one distillery, blended from many. Drunk neat or with a splash of water, which opens it up; ice is considered waste. Ask for a dram and describe what you like — smoky, sweet, coastal — rather than a brand.

Oats cooked slowly in water with salt — not milk, not sugar, if you follow the old rule — and eaten from a bowl. Scotland lived on this for centuries. There is a world championship for it, held every year in Carrbridge.

A rich fruit cake soaked in whisky and topped with concentric rings of blanched almonds, made without cherries by tradition. It began with a marmalade maker using up bitter orange peel. Keeps for months, improves for weeks.

Butter, sugar and flour in a ratio that is mostly butter, baked pale and dense. A good one snaps rather than bends and tastes of cream. Sold in tins to tourists everywhere — buy it from a bakery instead and eat it fresh.

A chocolate bar chilled, dipped in the batter meant for fish and fried until the inside turns to hot caramel. Invented in an Aberdeenshire chip shop in the 1990s as a joke that got away. Worth doing once, honestly.

Barley, root vegetables and lamb or beef simmered until thick enough to stand a spoon in. Less a starter than a meal that admits what it is. Every household version differs and every one is described as the correct one.

A small double-crusted pie of spiced mutton in a stiff hot-water pastry that stands up on its own, with a hollow rim built to hold beans or gravy. Sold at football grounds and bakeries. Eaten in one hand, standing up.

A dark, sweet cordial of grapes, raspberries, blackcurrants and herbs, invented in Manchester in 1908 as a health tonic and never adequately explained since. Drunk cold and diluted, or hot in winter. There is a statue to it.

A flat round of flaky pastry packed with currants, sugar and butter, the top slashed and sugared. Named for the town nearby and sold in every bakery. Eat it with a slice of crumbly Lancashire cheese, which is not a joke.

Shortcrust with a layer of raspberry jam, thick custard and desiccated coconut on top, often with a glacé cherry. The standard school pudding for generations, now on restaurant menus with a completely straight face.

Black peas boiled soft and served hot in a cup with malt vinegar, sold at bonfire night and at fairgrounds in early November. Older than the fireworks they go with. Cheap, salty and faintly odd, eaten outdoors in the cold.

Tripe simmered pale in milk with onions, once sold from dedicated tripe shops on every northern high street — Manchester had dozens. Now nearly extinct, kept alive at Bury market. Soft, mild, and historically enormous.

Beef and onion in suet pastry, tied in a cloth rag and boiled rather than baked, which leaves the pastry soft and slightly slippery. From Oldham, and rarer every year. Worth seeking where they still make their own.

Shortcrust filled with sharp cheese, onion and potato, eaten hot with gravy or cold from a paper bag. Every northern bakery makes one and every family argues about the potato. Vegetarian by accident rather than design.

Lamb and onions layered under sliced potato and baked slowly until the top browns and the bottom turns to gravy. Made in a tall pot in the mill towns, left to cook while everyone was at work. Pickled red cabbage on the side.

Thick-cut chips buried in beef gravy with a barm — the northern word for a soft bread roll — alongside, or built into a sandwich around the chips. Cheap, hot and unrepentant. The regional test of any chip shop.

Beer that finishes fermenting in the barrel and is pulled by hand pump, served cool rather than cold and with no added gas. Softer and flatter than most visitors expect. Ask for a pint of bitter and drink it slowly.

Banana, toffee made by boiling a can of condensed milk, and whipped cream on a biscuit base. Invented in a Sussex pub in 1971 and named by welding the two main ingredients together. The most 1970s dessert imaginable.

A coiled sweet dough with currants, lemon peel and spice, glazed sticky and pulled apart in a spiral. Sold from a Chelsea bakery from the 1700s that royalty lined up at. Eat it warm, the day it is baked, or not at all.

A dark sponge dense with chopped dates, drowned in hot toffee sauce and served with cream or custard. It tastes several centuries old and dates to the 1970s. Order it after a large meal; that is the accepted practice.

Broken meringue, whipped cream and crushed strawberries stirred into deliberate wreckage. Named for the school, where it was served at cricket matches. Best in June and July, when English strawberries are actually in season.

Smoked haddock, rice, curry spice, hard-boiled egg and parsley, eaten at breakfast. Anglo-Indian by birth, carried home by colonial officials and adopted by Victorian country houses. It sounds strange and works completely.

Eels chopped and boiled with their bones, then set in the savory jelly their own stock makes as it cools. Eaten cold with vinegar and white pepper. East End food, once daily, now defiantly rare. Genuinely not for everyone.

Roasted meat, potatoes crisped in fat, vegetables, gravy, and a Yorkshire pudding — a hollow baked batter built to catch the gravy. Served in pubs from noon until about four on Sundays and at no other time. Book, or go early.

A soft-boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat, breaded and fried, eaten cold in one hand. A London grocer claimed the invention in 1738. The good ones have a yolk that still runs; the bad ones are grey the whole way through.

Brisket cured in brine, boiled, and piled hot into a boiled-then-baked bagel with mustard and a pickled cucumber. From the Jewish East End and sold around the clock on Brick Lane. Order salt beef, not pastrami — they differ.

Minced beef pie, mashed potato, and liquor — a green parsley sauce, not alcohol — in tiled shops unchanged for a century. Cheap, plain, and vanishing: only a handful of the old family shops are still trading.

White fish in beer batter fried until it blisters, with thick-cut chips and mushy peas. Salt and malt vinegar go on at the counter, not the table. Ask for it wrapped, and a good piece will steam when you break it open.

Fried eggs, bacon, sausage, black pudding, beans, tomato, mushrooms and fried bread, all on one plate at once. Built for people about to do physical work and eaten mostly by people who are not. Tea alongside, not coffee.

Sangiovese from the hills between Florence and Siena, tart and dusty and built for food rather than sipping. The straw-covered flask is a tourist relic; the good bottles are not. Order the house red and this is usually what arrives.

Florence claims to have invented it at the Medici court in the 1500s, and the pale yellow flavor called Buontalenti is named for the man given credit. Look for muted colors and covered metal tubs — bright peaks mean air and additives.

Cold white wine from the volcanic hills southeast of the city, poured by the liter in old trattorias and drunk without ceremony. Not a wine to think about — it is what Romans drink with fried artichokes and pasta.

Cured pork jowl rendered crisp, then egg yolk and pecorino stirred in off the heat until they thicken without scrambling. No cream, ever, and no bacon. The pepper goes on heavily at the end, and the timing is everything.

Raw tomato, cucumber, pepper, garlic and bread blended cold with oil and vinegar into something closer to a drink than a soup. Served in a glass through the summer. What is sold abroad under the name is usually salsa by comparison.

Ridged batter piped into hot oil and fried crisp, with chocolate thick enough to stand a spoon in — for dipping, not drinking. Eaten at dawn after a long night, or at six in the afternoon. Never for dessert.

Fried potato chunks under a smoky, faintly hot red sauce built on paprika rather than tomato. The Madrid version is that sauce alone; the aioli one belongs elsewhere. A bar that gets these right usually gets everything right.

Sparkling wine made by the same slow method as Champagne, in cellars an hour outside the city, and drunk casually rather than saved for celebrations. A cold glass costs a couple of euros. Ask for brut nature if you want it bone dry.

Grilled bread rubbed with a cut tomato until the crumb turns pink, then olive oil and salt. Not a topping — the tomato is crushed into the bread and the skin thrown away. It arrives before everything else and costs almost nothing.

Tomato, buffalo mozzarella, basil and nothing else, baked ninety seconds in a wood oven until the rim blisters black and the center stays soupy. Naples invented this and protects it by law. Fold it in quarters if you are standing.

Thick, tart, almost chalky cultured dairy Icelanders have eaten for a thousand years — technically a soft cheese rather than a yogurt, though nobody will correct you. Eaten with milk and sugar, or straight from the tub at a bus stop.

A veal cutlet pounded thin, breaded, and fried in butter until the crust puffs away from the meat in a golden blister. Austrian law reserves the name for veal; pork versions must say so. Squeeze the lemon, eat it with potato salad, skip the sauce.
